exam1.question: In a normal second-trimester fetus, the cardiac axis measured on the four-chamber view is approximately how many degrees to the left of the anteroposterior midline of the thorax?

options.text: 10 degrees, plus or minus about 5 degrees
75 degrees, plus or minus about 5 degrees
90 degrees, plus or minus about 10 degrees
45 degrees, plus or minus about 20 degrees

exam1.explanation: The normal cardiac axis is about 45 degrees (range roughly 25 to 65 degrees) to the left of midline. An axis that is markedly increased, such as near 75 to 90 degrees, is associated with conotruncal anomalies and should prompt a detailed evaluation.
exam1.hint: Draw the line along the interventricular septum and compare it with a line from the spine to the sternum; a normal heart points toward the left anterior chest but is neither vertical nor horizontal.

exam1.question: The ductus venosus connects which two structures?

options.text: Pulmonary artery to the descending aorta
Portal vein to the hepatic artery
Umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava
Right atrium to the left atrium

exam1.explanation: The ductus venosus carries well-oxygenated blood from the intra-abdominal umbilical vein directly to the IVC, bypassing the liver. The pulmonary artery to aorta connection is the ductus arteriosus.
exam1.hint: Its name tells you it is part of the venous side of the fetal circulation in the liver.

exam1.question: In classic postnatal series, which type of ventricular septal defect is most common overall?
exam1.explanation: Perimembranous defects account for the majority (about 70 to 80 percent) of VSDs in postnatal series. Small muscular defects are frequently found prenatally but many close spontaneously.
exam1.hint: The defect involves the thin fibrous portion of the septum beneath the aortic valve.

exam1.question: Which of the four classic components of tetralogy of Fallot is usually NOT evident on prenatal ultrasound?
exam1.explanation: Right ventricular hypertrophy develops postnatally as the RV pumps against pulmonary obstruction at systemic pressures; in the fetus the ventricles are nearly equal in pressure, so hypertrophy is usually absent.
exam1.hint: Consider which feature is a secondary consequence of postnatal pressure loading.

exam1.question: In hypoplastic left heart syndrome with aortic atresia, which flow pattern is expected in the transverse aortic arch?

options.text: Retrograde flow supplied from the ductus arteriosus
Antegrade flow from the left ventricle
Absent flow throughout the cardiac cycle

exam1.explanation: With aortic atresia, the ductus supplies the arch and ascending aorta retrogradely to perfuse the head and coronary arteries. Antegrade flow from the left ventricle is absent.
exam1.hint: The ascending aorta must be filled from the ductal end.

exam1.question: What is the generally accepted normal baseline fetal heart rate range in the second and third trimesters?
exam1.explanation: A baseline of 110 to 160 bpm is the most widely cited normal range (some texts use 120 to 160). Sustained rates above 180 suggest tachyarrhythmia, and below 110 bradycardia.
exam1.hint: The normal range is faster than an adult rate but well below tachyarrhythmia thresholds.

exam1.question: In the third trimester, a fetus of a mother with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes shows thickening of the interventricular septum. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy related to maternal diabetes

exam1.explanation: Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes myocardial hypertrophy, most prominent in the septum, which usually regresses after birth. Rhabdomyomas appear as discrete masses.
exam1.hint: Fetal insulin acts as a growth factor for the myocardium.

exam1.question: According to widely used guidelines, what is the optimal gestational age for a comprehensive transabdominal fetal echocardiogram?
exam1.explanation: Most guidelines recommend 18 to 22 weeks, when the heart is large enough to evaluate and imaging is not yet limited by fetal position and rib shadowing. Earlier scans may need follow-up.
exam1.hint: This window coincides with the routine anatomy survey.

exam1.question: On a normal four-chamber view, the fetal heart occupies approximately what fraction of the thoracic area?
exam1.explanation: The normal fetal heart fills roughly one-third of the thoracic area (cardiothoracic area ratio about 0.25 to 0.35). Two-thirds or more would indicate marked cardiomegaly.
exam1.hint: Compare the heart outline with the combined lung fields in the same axial slice; the lungs should dominate.

exam1.question: Which fetal vessel carries blood with the highest oxygen saturation?
exam1.explanation: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood returning from the placenta and has the highest saturation in the fetus. Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta.
exam1.hint: Trace blood flow beginning at the placenta.

exam1.question: Which type of ventricular septal defect has the highest rate of spontaneous closure in utero or in infancy?

options.text: Inlet VSD as part of an AV septal defect
Malalignment VSD of tetralogy of Fallot

exam1.explanation: Small muscular VSDs frequently close spontaneously as the muscular septum grows. Inlet and malalignment defects do not close spontaneously.
exam1.hint: Defects surrounded entirely by growing muscle have the best chance of closing.

exam1.question: Why is tetralogy of Fallot often missed when screening relies on the four-chamber view alone?

options.text: The ventricles are always markedly unequal
The heart rate is too fast to evaluate
The four-chamber view usually appears normal

exam1.explanation: TOF is an outflow tract lesion, and the four-chamber view is typically normal apart from a possible leftward axis. Outflow tract and three-vessel views are required to detect it.
exam1.hint: The defect is located above the level of the AV valves.

exam1.question: In hypoplastic left heart syndrome, what is the expected direction of flow across the foramen ovale?

options.text: Right to left only in systole

exam1.explanation: Pulmonary venous return cannot exit through the hypoplastic left heart, so it crosses the foramen ovale from left atrium to right atrium. Normal fetal flow is right to left.
exam1.hint: Pulmonary venous blood needs another exit from the left atrium.

exam1.question: For M-mode assessment of fetal rhythm, how should the cursor be positioned?

options.text: Through an atrial wall and a ventricular wall simultaneously

exam1.explanation: Placing the cursor through both an atrium and a ventricle records atrial and ventricular contractions on the same tracing, allowing the AV relationship and any block or premature beats to be assessed.
exam1.hint: Rhythm diagnosis requires timing both chambers in relation to each other.

exam1.question: Which form of maternal diabetes is an established indication for fetal echocardiography because of increased congenital heart disease risk?

options.text: Gestational diabetes diagnosed in the third trimester

exam1.explanation: Pregestational diabetes, with hyperglycemia during organogenesis, raises CHD risk and warrants fetal echo. Gestational diabetes diagnosed after the first trimester does not substantially increase structural defect risk.
exam1.hint: Cardiac structures form in the first trimester.

exam1.question: In a high-risk pregnancy, an early fetal echocardiogram using the transvaginal approach can be performed at about which gestational age?
exam1.explanation: Early fetal echo at roughly 12 to 16 weeks, often transvaginally, can detect major defects in high-risk patients, but a follow-up at 18 to 22 weeks is still recommended. At 6 to 8 weeks cardiac structures are too small.
exam1.hint: Early scanning is feasible near the end of the first trimester when the heart is just resolvable.

exam1.question: Which cardiac chamber lies closest to the anterior chest wall in the normal fetal four-chamber view?
exam1.explanation: The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber, lying directly behind the sternum. The left atrium is the most posterior chamber, closest to the spine and descending aorta.
exam1.hint: Think about which chamber is farthest from the spine.

exam1.question: Preferential streaming in the fetal inferior vena cava directs well-oxygenated ductus venosus blood primarily toward which destination?

options.text: Through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle
Across the foramen ovale into the left atrium

exam1.explanation: The crista dividens directs the high-velocity ductus venosus stream across the foramen ovale to the left heart, supplying the coronary and cerebral circulations with the most oxygenated blood. Deoxygenated SVC blood is directed mainly toward the tricuspid valve.
exam1.hint: The most oxygenated blood is routed toward the heart and brain.

exam1.question: An inlet ventricular septal defect is located beneath which structures and is typically part of which lesion?

options.text: Beneath the semilunar valves; part of truncus arteriosus
Beneath the AV valves; part of an atrioventricular septal defect
At the apex; part of hypoplastic left heart
Beneath the aortic valve; part of coarctation

exam1.explanation: The inlet septum lies beneath the AV valves, and inlet VSDs are the ventricular component of AV septal (canal) defects. Defects beneath the semilunar valves are outlet defects.
exam1.hint: Inlet refers to the portion of the septum separating the ventricular inflows.

exam1.question: What is the hallmark finding of tetralogy of Fallot on the left ventricular outflow tract (five-chamber) view?

options.text: Aorta arising entirely from the right ventricle anteriorly
A malalignment VSD with the aorta overriding the septum
A single great artery giving off the pulmonary arteries
Parallel great arteries with the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle

exam1.explanation: Anterior malalignment of the outlet septum creates a VSD over which a dilated aorta overrides. A single trunk giving off the pulmonary arteries describes truncus arteriosus.
exam1.hint: Look at how the anterior aortic wall relates to the ventricular septum.

exam1.question: In a fetus with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, pulmonary venous Doppler shows prominent reversed flow during atrial contraction. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A restrictive or intact atrial septum
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return below the diaphragm

exam1.explanation: When left atrial egress is restricted, left atrial pressure rises and pulmonary venous flow shows large reversal with atrial contraction and reduced forward flow. Restrictive septum in HLHS carries high neonatal mortality and may require urgent intervention.
exam1.hint: Pulmonary venous reversal reflects pressure in the chamber the veins drain into.

exam1.question: Using simultaneous Doppler of left ventricular inflow and outflow, the interval from onset of the mitral A wave to onset of aortic ejection represents what?
exam1.explanation: The time from atrial contraction (A wave onset) to ventricular ejection approximates the PR interval and is used to monitor for first-degree heart block, particularly in anti-Ro exposed pregnancies.
exam1.hint: The interval spans from atrial contraction to the start of ventricular outflow.

exam1.question: First-trimester maternal lithium exposure has classically been associated with which cardiac defect?
exam1.explanation: Lithium has historically been linked to Ebstein anomaly, although more recent data suggest the absolute risk is lower than first reported. It remains a classic teaching association.
exam1.hint: The association involves the tricuspid valve.

exam1.question: Which adjustment most effectively increases frame rate for fetal cardiac imaging?

options.text: Increasing the number of focal zones
Widening the color box to include the entire thorax
Narrowing the sector width and reducing depth to the heart

exam1.explanation: Frame rate improves when fewer scan lines and shorter round-trip times are needed, so a narrow sector and minimal depth help. Multiple focal zones and higher line density reduce frame rate.
exam1.hint: Frame rate depends on how many pulses must be sent and how long each takes to return.

exam1.question: A prominent muscular band crossing from the interventricular septum to the free wall near the apex identifies which chamber?
exam1.explanation: The moderator band is a hallmark of the morphologic right ventricle, along with coarse trabeculations and apical insertion of its AV valve. The morphologic left ventricle has a smooth wall and a bullet-shaped apex.
exam1.hint: This band carries part of the right bundle branch and is used to assign ventricular identity.

exam1.question: The ductus arteriosus connects the main pulmonary artery to which vessel?

options.text: Descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery
Ascending aorta proximal to the brachiocephalic artery

exam1.explanation: The ductus arteriosus joins the main pulmonary artery to the descending aorta just beyond the left subclavian artery origin, allowing most right ventricular output to bypass the lungs.
exam1.hint: The ductal arch joins the aorta beyond the head and neck branches.

exam1.question: A ventricular septal defect located immediately beneath both the aortic and pulmonary valves is classified as which type?
exam1.explanation: Doubly committed subarterial VSDs lie in the outlet septum directly beneath both semilunar valves and can lead to aortic cusp prolapse. Perimembranous defects lie beneath the aortic valve adjacent to the tricuspid valve.
exam1.hint: The defect sits where the outflow septum should separate both arterial valves.
keywords: both the aortic and pulmonary valves

exam1.question: A fetus has a VSD with an overriding aorta, markedly dilated branch pulmonary arteries and to-and-fro flow across a rudimentary pulmonary valve. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.text: Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia
Critical pulmonary stenosis with intact septum
Tetralogy of Fallot with absent pulmonary valve

exam1.explanation: Absent pulmonary valve syndrome shows a rudimentary valve ring with stenosis and free regurgitation, causing aneurysmal pulmonary arteries that can compress the airways. Pulmonary atresia would show no antegrade flow and small pulmonary arteries.
exam1.hint: Free regurgitation into the pulmonary arteries produces a characteristic size change.

exam1.question: A bright, echogenic lining of the left ventricular endocardium in a fetus with critical aortic stenosis most likely represents what?
exam1.explanation: Endocardial fibroelastosis is diffuse echogenic thickening of the endocardium from chronic pressure overload and ischemia, typical of critical aortic stenosis and evolving HLHS. Rhabdomyomas are discrete masses.
exam1.hint: The finding is diffuse along the chamber lining rather than a discrete mass.

exam1.question: What is the most common fetal arrhythmia?
exam1.explanation: Premature atrial contractions are by far the most common fetal arrhythmia and are usually benign, often resolving spontaneously. A small proportion progress to SVT.
exam1.hint: The most frequent rhythm irregularity is also the most benign.

exam1.question: Maternal isotretinoin (retinoic acid) use is most strongly associated with which group of heart defects?
exam1.explanation: Retinoic acid interferes with neural crest cell migration and is associated with conotruncal and aortic arch anomalies. It does not cause cardiac tumors.
exam1.hint: Neural crest cells contribute to outflow tract septation.

exam1.question: To demonstrate low-velocity pulmonary venous flow into the left atrium with color Doppler, which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Raise the velocity scale above 80 cm/s
Increase the wall filter to maximum
Decrease color gain until no noise appears

exam1.explanation: Pulmonary venous velocities are low, so a lower scale (about 20 to 30 cm/s, commonly cited) and low wall filter improve sensitivity. A high scale or high wall filter will miss slow flow.
exam1.hint: Slow flow needs a color setting tuned to low velocities.

exam1.question: In the normal four-chamber view, how does the insertion of the tricuspid valve compare with that of the mitral valve?

options.text: The mitral valve inserts slightly more apically than the tricuspid valve
Both valves insert at exactly the same level on the septum
The tricuspid valve inserts on the atrial septum above the mitral valve
The tricuspid valve inserts slightly more apically than the mitral valve

exam1.explanation: Normal AV valve offset places the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve a few millimeters closer to the apex than the mitral valve. Loss of this offset (linear insertion) suggests an AV septal defect, while exaggerated displacement suggests Ebstein anomaly.
exam1.hint: Normal offset is lost in a canal defect and exaggerated in Ebstein anomaly.

exam1.question: Which describes a normal second-trimester ductus venosus Doppler waveform?

options.text: Continuous flat flow with no phasic variation
Forward flow throughout the cardiac cycle, including during atrial contraction
Forward flow in systole with absent flow in diastole

exam1.explanation: The normal ductus venosus shows forward flow with S, D and a waves all above baseline. An absent or reversed a wave indicates elevated right-sided filling pressure and is abnormal after the first trimester.
exam1.hint: Focus on the direction of the a wave, which reflects atrial contraction.

exam1.question: Why can an apical four-chamber view produce a false-positive ventricular septal defect?

options.text: The septum lies perpendicular to the beam, increasing reflections
The septum lies parallel to the beam, causing dropout of the thin membranous portion
Color gain is always too low in this view
The moderator band mimics a septal gap

exam1.explanation: When the beam runs parallel to the septum, weak specular reflection from the thin membranous septum causes echo dropout that mimics a defect. A subcostal or lateral view with the beam perpendicular to the septum is preferred.
exam1.hint: Specular reflectors return the strongest echoes at a particular angle of incidence.

exam1.question: Which aortic arch anomaly is found in roughly a quarter of patients with tetralogy of Fallot?
exam1.explanation: A right aortic arch occurs in about 25 percent of TOF cases and is a clue to look for 22q11 deletion. In the three-vessel-trachea view the arch passes to the right of the trachea.
exam1.hint: Check which side of the trachea the transverse arch passes in the three-vessel-trachea view.

exam1.question: A midgestation fetus has critical aortic stenosis with a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle, retrograde arch flow and left-to-right atrial flow. This pattern is most concerning for what?
exam1.explanation: Critical aortic stenosis with LV dysfunction, reversed arch flow and reversed atrial shunting predicts progression to HLHS, and such fetuses may be considered for fetal aortic valvuloplasty. Ebstein anomaly affects the right heart.
exam1.hint: The left ventricle is failing to sustain systemic output, and these flow reversals predict its growth.

exam1.question: A fetus has a heart rate of about 75 bpm. M-mode shows atrial contractions at about 150 per minute with every second atrial beat premature and not followed by a ventricular contraction. What is the diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: Premature atrial beats that are nonconducted in a bigeminal pattern halve the ventricular rate and mimic bradycardia. In complete heart block the atrial rate is regular and dissociated from the ventricles.
exam1.hint: Note whether the atrial beats are regularly spaced or early.

exam1.question: Interrupted aortic arch type B is most strongly associated with which genetic condition?
exam1.explanation: About half of patients with interrupted aortic arch type B (between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries) have 22q11.2 deletion. Turner syndrome is associated with coarctation.
exam1.hint: This deletion syndrome affects neural crest-derived arch arteries and the thymus.

exam1.question: Which adjustment reduces aliasing on pulsed wave Doppler of a high-velocity jet?

options.text: Increasing the depth of the sample volume
Increasing the pulse repetition frequency or shifting the baseline

exam1.explanation: Raising the PRF (scale) and moving the baseline increase the displayable velocity range. Higher transducer frequency and deeper sampling both worsen aliasing.
exam1.hint: Aliasing occurs when the Doppler shift exceeds half of the sampling rate.

exam1.question: In a normal fetus, the flap of the foramen ovale is seen moving into which chamber?
exam1.explanation: Normal right-to-left atrial shunting pushes the septum primum flap into the left atrium. A flap bowing into the right atrium suggests reversed shunting, as in left heart obstruction.
exam1.hint: Follow the direction of normal fetal atrial-level shunting.

exam1.question: How does the normal umbilical artery Doppler waveform change as pregnancy advances?

options.text: Diastolic flow increases and the S/D ratio decreases
Diastolic flow decreases and the S/D ratio increases
End-diastolic flow becomes absent after 30 weeks

exam1.explanation: Placental vascular resistance falls with gestation, so end-diastolic flow rises and the S/D ratio and pulsatility index fall. Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow is abnormal at any viable gestation.
exam1.hint: Think about what happens to placental resistance as the villous vascular bed expands.

exam1.question: What flow pattern is typical across an isolated ventricular septal defect in the fetus?

options.text: No flow because the defect is closed by pressure

exam1.explanation: Right and left ventricular pressures are nearly equal in the fetus, so VSD flow is low velocity and often bidirectional. High-velocity left-to-right jets typically appear only after birth when pulmonary resistance falls.
exam1.hint: Compare fetal right and left ventricular pressures with postnatal pressures.

exam1.question: In tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia, pulmonary blood flow may be supplied by which vessels arising from the descending aorta?
exam1.explanation: MAPCAs arising from the descending aorta can supply the lungs when the pulmonary arteries are small or discontinuous. Coronary fistulas are more associated with pulmonary atresia with intact septum.
exam1.hint: Look for small arterial branches heading from the descending thoracic aorta toward the lungs.

exam1.question: Which is the most common prenatal clue to coarctation of the aorta?

options.text: Left ventricle larger than right ventricle
A dilated ascending aorta with a normal arch
Ventricular and great artery disproportion with the right side larger
Absent flow in the ductus arteriosus

exam1.explanation: Coarctation typically shows a smaller left ventricle and aorta relative to the right ventricle and pulmonary artery, often with a hypoplastic transverse arch or isthmus. Prenatal diagnosis remains challenging because the ductus is open.
exam1.hint: Look for asymmetry between the two sides of the heart and great arteries.

exam1.question: Which finding is typical of fetal supraventricular tachycardia?

options.text: An atrial rate of about 400 to 500 bpm with 2:1 block
A ventricular rate of about 220 to 300 bpm with 1:1 AV conduction
AV dissociation with a slow ventricular rate

exam1.explanation: Fetal SVT typically shows a regular rate of about 220 to 300 bpm with each atrial beat conducted. Atrial rates of 400 to 500 with block indicate atrial flutter.
exam1.hint: Count the ratio of atrial to ventricular contractions.

exam1.question: Which cardiac lesions are most associated with Turner syndrome (45,X)?

options.text: Coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve
Tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus

exam1.explanation: Turner syndrome is classically associated with left-sided obstructive lesions, including coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve and HLHS, often with cystic hygroma. AVSD is the hallmark of trisomy 21.
exam1.hint: Turner syndrome favors left-sided obstruction.

exam1.question: For accurate spectral Doppler velocity measurement across a fetal cardiac valve, what is the preferred angle of insonation?

options.text: As close to 0 degrees as possible, ideally under 20 degrees
Any angle, because velocity is angle independent

exam1.explanation: In fetal echo, flow should be interrogated nearly parallel to the beam, with angles under about 20 degrees, so cosine error is minimal. At 90 degrees no Doppler shift is detected.
exam1.hint: The Doppler shift is proportional to the cosine of the angle.

exam1.question: Which statement about pulmonary venous return is expected on a normal fetal four-chamber view?

options.text: Pulmonary veins drain into the coronary sinus
A confluence is seen behind the left atrium draining upward
The pulmonary veins enter the right atrium near the SVC
At least two pulmonary veins are seen entering the left atrium

exam1.explanation: Normally at least two pulmonary veins, usually the right and left lower veins, are demonstrated entering the posterior left atrium, often confirmed with low-velocity color Doppler. A separate confluence behind the left atrium suggests anomalous pulmonary venous return.
exam1.hint: Use low-scale color Doppler at the posterior wall of the most posterior chamber.

exam1.question: In a growth-restricted fetus, which middle cerebral artery Doppler change indicates brain-sparing redistribution?

options.text: Absent diastolic flow with a higher pulsatility index
Increased diastolic flow with a lower pulsatility index
Unchanged diastolic flow with higher systolic velocity

exam1.explanation: The MCA is normally a high-resistance vessel; cerebral vasodilation in hypoxemia increases diastolic flow and lowers the PI. Absent diastolic flow is the normal high-resistance direction, not redistribution.
exam1.hint: Vasodilation lowers resistance, which changes the diastolic component.

exam1.question: Why is a secundum atrial septal defect rarely diagnosed prenatally?

options.text: The atrial septum is not visible before birth
The foramen ovale is normally patent, so the defect is hard to distinguish
Secundum defects only form after birth
Color Doppler cannot be used at the atrial level

exam1.explanation: Because the foramen ovale normally allows right-to-left flow in the same region, a secundum ASD is difficult to separate from the normal opening. Most are diagnosed postnatally.
exam1.hint: Think about which normal fetal opening sits in the middle of the atrial septum.

exam1.question: In a fetus with tetralogy of Fallot, reversed flow in the ductus arteriosus (from aorta to pulmonary artery) indicates what?

options.text: Severe RVOT obstruction with ductal-dependent pulmonary circulation
Mild pulmonary stenosis with no clinical concern

exam1.explanation: Retrograde ductal flow means the lungs are being supplied from the aorta because antegrade pulmonary flow is severely limited, so prostaglandin will be needed at birth. Ductal-dependent systemic circulation occurs in left-sided obstruction such as HLHS.
exam1.hint: Ask which circulation the ductus is supplying when its flow reverses.

exam1.question: Where is coarctation of the aorta most commonly located?

options.text: At the aortic isthmus near the ductal insertion, distal to the left subclavian artery
At the aortic root just above the valve
In the abdominal aorta near the renal arteries
Between the brachiocephalic and left carotid arteries

exam1.explanation: Coarctation is typically juxtaductal at the isthmus, between the left subclavian artery and the ductus arteriosus. Supravalvular narrowing near the root is a different lesion.
exam1.hint: The narrowing relates to ductal tissue extending into the aortic wall.

exam1.question: Which finding is typical of fetal atrial flutter?

options.text: An atrial rate of 120 bpm with a ventricular rate of 60 bpm
Irregular ventricular beats with compensatory pauses
An atrial rate of about 300 to 500 bpm with variable AV block, often 2:1

exam1.explanation: Atrial flutter produces very rapid regular atrial activity with AV block, so the ventricular rate is lower, commonly about 220 to 240 bpm with 2:1 conduction. A 1:1 ratio is more typical of SVT.
exam1.hint: The atrial rate is much faster than the ventricular rate.

exam1.question: Which cardiac pattern is characteristic of trisomy 18?
exam1.explanation: Most fetuses with trisomy 18 have heart defects, typically VSD with thickened, dysplastic valves involving more than one valve; DORV is also common. Rhabdomyomas suggest tuberous sclerosis.
exam1.hint: Multiple valves are typically affected.

exam1.question: Why is tissue harmonic imaging useful in fetal echocardiography of patients with a high body mass index?

options.text: It increases the frame rate dramatically
It increases penetration by using a higher transmit frequency
It reduces near-field artifacts and improves contrast resolution
It eliminates the need for Doppler

exam1.explanation: Harmonic imaging uses frequencies generated within tissue, reducing reverberation and clutter from the abdominal wall and improving endocardial border definition. It does not increase frame rate.
exam1.hint: Harmonic frequencies are generated as the beam travels through tissue rather than at the skin surface.

exam1.question: On a normal four-chamber view, which vessel is seen in cross section between the left atrium and the spine, slightly to the left of midline?
exam1.explanation: The descending aorta lies posterior to the left atrium and just left of the spine. A second vessel beside it in this location may be a dilated azygos vein, as in interrupted IVC with azygos continuation.
exam1.hint: This is the vessel the ductal and aortic arches join.

exam1.question: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is used to screen for fetal anemia. Which threshold is most widely used to suggest moderate to severe anemia?

options.text: Greater than 1.5 multiples of the median
Greater than 0.5 multiples of the median
Greater than 1.0 multiples of the median
Less than 1.5 multiples of the median

exam1.explanation: An MCA PSV above 1.5 MoM for gestational age is the widely taught threshold for moderate to severe anemia, reflecting lower viscosity and increased cardiac output. Values near 1.0 MoM are normal.
exam1.hint: Anemia lowers blood viscosity and raises velocity, so look for a value well above the median.

exam1.question: A primum atrial septal defect is located in which part of the atrial septum?

options.text: The upper portion near the SVC entry
The central portion at the fossa ovalis
The posterior portion near the coronary sinus ostium only
The lower portion adjacent to the AV valves

exam1.explanation: A primum ASD lies in the lowest part of the atrial septum adjacent to the AV valves and is the atrial component of a partial AV septal defect, often with a cleft mitral valve. A defect near the SVC is a sinus venosus defect.
exam1.hint: This defect belongs to the endocardial cushion family.

exam1.question: In dextro-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA), which ventricular-arterial connection is present?

options.text: Aorta from the left ventricle and pulmonary artery from the right ventricle
Both great arteries from the right ventricle
A single great artery from both ventricles
Aorta from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle

exam1.explanation: D-TGA has ventriculoarterial discordance with concordant AV connections, creating parallel circulations. Both arteries from the right ventricle describes DORV.
exam1.hint: Transposition means the great arteries are switched relative to their normal ventricles.

exam1.question: A third-trimester fetus has a right ventricle slightly larger than the left with otherwise normal anatomy and arch dimensions. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: It is diagnostic of hypoplastic left heart
Mild right-sided dominance can be normal in the third trimester
It indicates total anomalous pulmonary venous return

exam1.explanation: Mild right ventricular dominance is physiologic late in gestation, making isolated disproportion a common false-positive sign of coarctation. Diagnosis relies on arch measurements and other findings.
exam1.hint: Consider the normal change in ventricular proportions with gestational age.

exam1.question: What is the most common mechanism of fetal supraventricular tachycardia?

options.text: Atrioventricular reentry through an accessory pathway

exam1.explanation: Most fetal SVT is AV reentrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway, producing a short ventriculoatrial interval. Junctional ectopic tachycardia is rare.
exam1.hint: Consider a reentry circuit that uses an extra electrical connection.

exam1.question: Which cardiac lesion is most characteristic of Noonan syndrome?
exam1.explanation: Noonan syndrome is classically associated with pulmonary stenosis from a dysplastic valve and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Supravalvular aortic stenosis is characteristic of Williams syndrome.
exam1.hint: This RASopathy commonly affects the right ventricular outflow valve.

exam1.question: What persistence setting is preferred when imaging the fetal heart?

options.text: Persistence has no effect on cardiac imaging

exam1.explanation: Persistence averages successive frames and blurs rapidly moving structures such as valve leaflets, so low persistence is preferred for the fetal heart. High persistence suits slow-moving abdominal anatomy.
exam1.hint: Frame averaging trades temporal resolution for a smoother image.

exam1.question: Which describes the normal spatial relationship of the great arteries as they leave the heart?

options.text: They run parallel, with the aorta anterior and to the right
They run parallel, with the pulmonary artery to the right
They arise side by side from the right ventricle
They cross each other, with the pulmonary artery passing anterior to the aorta

exam1.explanation: Normally the outflow tracts cross: the pulmonary artery leaves the anterior right ventricle and courses leftward over the aorta, which arises from the left ventricle. Parallel great arteries suggest transposition or double outlet right ventricle.
exam1.hint: Sweeping cranially from the five-chamber view, the outflow tracts should form a crossing pattern.

exam1.question: What is the normal fetal atrioventricular valve inflow pattern on pulsed Doppler?

options.text: Biphasic with the E wave taller than the A wave
Biphasic with the A wave taller than the E wave
Biphasic with reversed flow during atrial contraction

exam1.explanation: Fetal ventricular relaxation is immature, so atrial contraction contributes more to filling and the A wave exceeds the E wave (E/A less than 1). The E/A ratio rises toward 1 with advancing gestation; E greater than A is the adult pattern.
exam1.hint: The fetal myocardium is stiffer than the adult myocardium, so active filling dominates.

exam1.question: Which is the hallmark finding of a complete atrioventricular septal defect on the four-chamber view?

options.text: Marked apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
A common AV valve with loss of normal offset
An isolated small apical muscular defect

exam1.explanation: A complete AVSD shows a common AV valve bridging both ventricles at the same level, with a primum atrial and inlet ventricular defect forming a central cross defect. Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve is Ebstein anomaly.
exam1.hint: Look at the crux of the heart where the two AV valves normally insert at slightly different levels.

exam1.question: In typical D-TGA, where is the aorta positioned relative to the pulmonary artery?
exam1.explanation: In D-TGA the aorta usually lies anterior and rightward of the pulmonary artery, and the vessels run parallel. In normal hearts the aorta is posterior and rightward.
exam1.hint: The D refers to the direction of the ventricular loop and arterial position.

exam1.question: Which finding is typical of fetal valvar aortic stenosis?

options.text: A thickened, doming aortic valve with increased velocity and turbulent flow
An absent aortic valve with to-and-fro flow
A normal aortic valve with low velocity
A dilated aortic root with no flow

exam1.explanation: Valvar aortic stenosis shows thickened, doming leaflets and an elevated, aliasing jet on Doppler. In severe forms with LV dysfunction the gradient may be underestimated.
exam1.hint: Obstruction causes flow acceleration distal to the narrowed orifice.

exam1.question: Which medication is most commonly used as first-line transplacental therapy for sustained fetal SVT without hydrops?
exam1.explanation: Digoxin has traditionally been the most common first-line agent for nonhydropic fetal SVT, with flecainide or sotalol used as alternatives or when hydrops impairs placental transfer. Protocols vary by center.
exam1.hint: Choose the oral maternal agent with the longest track record for SVT without hydrops, remembering that placental transfer of this drug drops sharply once hydrops develops.

exam1.question: Supravalvular aortic stenosis is classically associated with which syndrome?
exam1.explanation: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene) causes supravalvular aortic stenosis and peripheral pulmonary stenosis. Holt-Oram is associated with septal defects and limb anomalies.
exam1.hint: The causative deletion involves the elastin gene.

exam1.question: When recording ventricular inflow with pulsed Doppler, where should the sample volume be placed?

options.text: In the mid atrium above the AV valve
Just distal to the AV valve leaflet tips in the ventricle
In the outflow tract beyond the semilunar valve

exam1.explanation: AV valve inflow is best recorded with the sample volume just beyond the leaflet tips on the ventricular side, where the E and A waves are best defined. Sampling in the atrium or apex distorts the pattern.
exam1.hint: Sample where the inflow stream is narrowest and fastest during diastole.

exam1.question: In the normal three-vessel view, what is the order of vessels from the fetal left to the fetal right?

options.text: Aorta, pulmonary artery, superior vena cava
Pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava
Superior vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery
Pulmonary artery, superior vena cava, aorta

exam1.explanation: From left to right the vessels are the pulmonary artery, aorta and SVC, and their diameters normally decrease in that order. An abnormal order, number or size suggests conotruncal or arch anomalies.
exam1.hint: The largest vessel is the most leftward and anterior, and size decreases across the row.

exam1.question: Which statement about combined fetal cardiac output is correct?

options.text: The right ventricle ejects slightly more than the left, about 55 to 60 percent
The left ventricle ejects about 75 percent of combined output
The right ventricle ejects about 90 percent of combined output

exam1.explanation: The fetal heart works in parallel, and the right ventricle is mildly dominant at about 55 to 60 percent of combined output. This explains mild normal right-sided dominance late in gestation.
exam1.hint: The fetal ventricles pump in parallel rather than in series, and one has a modest edge.

exam1.question: In a fetus with an atrioventricular septal defect, which chromosomal abnormality is most commonly found?
exam1.explanation: Roughly 40 to 50 percent of fetuses with AVSD have trisomy 21. Monosomy X is more typically associated with left-sided obstructive lesions such as coarctation.
exam1.hint: This lesion is the classic cardiac marker of the most common autosomal trisomy in live births.

exam1.question: Which three-vessel view finding is characteristic of D-TGA?

options.text: Four vessels are seen, with an extra vessel left of the pulmonary artery
The normal pulmonary artery, aorta and SVC are in normal order
A dilated pulmonary artery with a small aorta to its left
Only two vessels are seen, with the transverse aorta anterior and the pulmonary artery at a lower level

exam1.explanation: Because the arteries run parallel, the three-vessel-trachea view typically shows only the aorta and SVC, sometimes as an I sign, with the pulmonary artery bifurcating at a lower level. An extra vessel left of the pulmonary artery suggests a persistent left SVC.
exam1.hint: Parallel vessels cannot be seen side by side in the same plane as in a normal crossing pattern.

exam1.question: In pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum, which finding has major prognostic importance?

options.text: A persistent left superior vena cava
Right ventricle to coronary artery sinusoids or fistulas

exam1.explanation: A hypertensive, hypoplastic RV can decompress through coronary sinusoids; RV-dependent coronary circulation affects surgical options and prognosis. A right aortic arch is not a major determinant.
exam1.hint: Ask where blood goes when a hypertensive right ventricle has no outlet.
keywords: pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

exam1.question: Which M-mode finding is diagnostic of complete (third-degree) heart block?

options.text: Every atrial beat followed by a ventricular beat at 150 bpm
Normal-rate atrial contractions completely dissociated from slower ventricular contractions
Atrial contractions faster than ventricular in a fixed 2:1 ratio
Occasional early atrial beats with pauses

exam1.explanation: Complete heart block shows atrial and ventricular contractions with no relationship, the ventricular rate typically 50 to 80 bpm. A fixed 2:1 ratio indicates second-degree block.
exam1.hint: In this rhythm the two chambers beat independently.

exam1.question: Multiple homogeneous echogenic masses within the ventricles and septum of a fetus are most likely rhabdomyomas. Which condition should then be evaluated?
exam1.explanation: Rhabdomyoma is the most common fetal cardiac tumor, and multiple tumors carry a high association with tuberous sclerosis complex, so fetal brain MRI and genetic testing are recommended. Beckwith-Wiedemann is not a classic association.
exam1.hint: Multiple tumors of this type point to an autosomal dominant hamartoma syndrome, so the workup extends to the fetal brain.

exam1.question: Which statement best describes the STIC (spatiotemporal correlation) acquisition technique?

options.text: A slow automated sweep acquires a volume that is reconstructed into one cardiac cycle
A single 2D frame is reconstructed into 3D using M-mode
Multiple manual sweeps are combined by the sonographer
It uses ECG gating from a fetal electrode

exam1.explanation: STIC performs a single automated sweep over several seconds, then uses detected systolic peaks to reconstruct a volume representing one cardiac cycle that can be reviewed in any plane. No fetal ECG is needed.
exam1.hint: The system detects periodic motion of the heart to sort frames by cardiac phase.

exam1.question: In a normal three-vessel-trachea view, where do the transverse aortic arch and the ductal arch lie relative to the trachea?

options.text: Both lie to the right of the trachea
The aortic arch lies right and the ductus left, forming a U shape
The aortic arch lies left and the ductus right of the trachea
Both lie to the left of the trachea, forming a V shape

exam1.explanation: Normally both arches converge to the left of the trachea in a V configuration. A U shape with the trachea enclosed between a right aortic arch and a left ductus indicates a vascular ring.
exam1.hint: Locate the echogenic ring of the trachea and note which side the converging arches sit on.

exam1.question: Why does most of the fetal right ventricular output bypass the lungs?

options.text: The pulmonary valve is functionally closed
The foramen ovale diverts it before the ventricle

exam1.explanation: Fluid-filled lungs and constricted pulmonary arterioles create high pulmonary vascular resistance, so most right ventricular output crosses the ductus arteriosus to the lower-resistance descending aorta and placenta.
exam1.hint: Blood follows the path of least resistance; compare the lungs with the placenta.

exam1.question: A fetus has a complete atrioventricular septal defect. Which additional finding most strongly suggests heterotaxy rather than trisomy 21 as the underlying cause?

options.text: Interrupted IVC with azygos continuation and complete heart block
A balanced AVSD with normal situs

exam1.explanation: An AVSD with abnormal situs, an interrupted IVC with azygos continuation and complete heart block suggests left atrial isomerism. An AVSD with normal situs and soft markers such as a thick nuchal fold or pyelectasis suggests trisomy 21.
exam1.hint: Check the abdominal situs and the venous anatomy as well as the heart itself.

exam1.question: What does the four-chamber view typically show in isolated D-TGA?
exam1.explanation: Isolated D-TGA has normal atria, ventricles and AV valves, so the four-chamber view usually appears normal. This is why outflow tract views are essential for detection.
exam1.hint: The abnormality is in how the outflow tracts connect, not in the inflow portion.

exam1.question: In pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum, how is the main pulmonary artery filled?

options.text: Retrograde flow from the ductus arteriosus
Antegrade flow through the pulmonary valve
Flow from the left ventricle across a VSD
Flow from the superior vena cava

exam1.explanation: With no antegrade outflow from the right ventricle, the pulmonary arteries fill retrogradely from the aorta through the ductus. Pulmonary circulation is therefore ductal dependent at birth.
exam1.hint: The pulmonary valve is closed, so the blood must come from the systemic side.
keywords: pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

exam1.question: Maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies place the fetus at greatest risk for developing heart block during which approximate gestational window?
exam1.explanation: Antibody-mediated injury of the conduction system most often occurs between about 16 and 26 weeks, so serial mechanical PR monitoring is usually performed in this window. Onset after 28 weeks is uncommon.
exam1.hint: The window coincides with transplacental IgG transfer during the midtrimester.

exam1.question: What is the typical natural history of fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas?

options.text: They steadily grow after birth and require resection in all cases
They calcify and rupture before birth
They may grow during pregnancy and then regress after birth

exam1.explanation: Rhabdomyomas often enlarge during the third trimester under maternal hormonal influence and tend to regress spontaneously in infancy. Surgery is reserved for obstruction or refractory arrhythmia.
exam1.hint: These hamartomas respond to the hormonal environment of pregnancy.

exam1.question: Which condition during acquisition most commonly degrades a STIC volume?

options.text: Using a low frame rate on the 2D image
Fetal movement or maternal breathing during the sweep

exam1.explanation: Because the volume is built over several seconds, fetal motion or maternal respiration introduces misregistration artifacts. Acquisition should be done with the fetus at rest and the mother holding her breath.
exam1.hint: Any motion other than the heartbeat during the sweep corrupts reconstruction.

exam1.question: Which feature distinguishes the aortic arch from the ductal arch in a sagittal view?

options.text: The aortic arch has a broad hockey-stick curve with no branches
The aortic arch has a tight candy-cane curve and gives rise to head and neck vessels
The aortic arch arises from the anterior ventricle
The aortic arch joins the descending aorta below the diaphragm

exam1.explanation: The aortic arch arises centrally in the chest with a tight curve and gives off the brachiocephalic, left carotid and left subclavian arteries. The ductal arch is flatter (hockey-stick shaped), arises more anteriorly and has no head and neck branches.
exam1.hint: Look for branching vessels heading toward the neck.

exam1.question: After birth, the foramen ovale closes functionally primarily because of which change?

options.text: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure
Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure

exam1.explanation: With lung expansion, pulmonary venous return increases left atrial pressure while loss of placental return lowers right atrial pressure, pressing the septum primum flap against the septum secundum.
exam1.hint: Consider which atrium gains volume when the lungs begin receiving blood.

exam1.question: In an unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect, which finding is present?

options.text: Both ventricles are equal in size
The AV valve offset is exaggerated
The common AV valve is committed mainly to one ventricle, which is dominant

exam1.explanation: In an unbalanced AVSD the common valve opens predominantly into one ventricle, leaving the other hypoplastic, which can preclude biventricular repair. Balanced defects have similarly sized ventricles.
exam1.hint: Compare the two ventricular sizes and how the common valve is shared.

exam1.question: In a fetus with D-TGA and an intact ventricular septum, which prenatal finding most suggests the need for urgent balloon atrial septostomy after birth?

options.text: A wide-open foramen ovale with bidirectional flow
A restrictive or hypermobile foramen ovale flap

exam1.explanation: Postnatal mixing in D-TGA depends on the atrial communication, and a restrictive or redundant, hypermobile foramen ovale predicts severe hypoxemia requiring urgent septostomy. A wide-open foramen allows adequate mixing.
exam1.hint: Survival after birth in parallel circulations depends on the size of the mixing site.

exam1.question: Which finding is characteristic of fetal valvar pulmonary stenosis?

options.text: A small, hypoplastic main pulmonary artery with retrograde flow
Absent pulmonary valve tissue with aneurysmal branches
A thickened, doming pulmonary valve with post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery
A pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle

exam1.explanation: Valvar pulmonary stenosis typically shows a thickened, doming valve with a high-velocity jet and post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery. A small pulmonary artery with retrograde ductal flow suggests atresia.
exam1.hint: A high-velocity jet distal to a narrowed valve expands the vessel downstream.

exam1.question: Complete heart block in a fetus with a structurally abnormal heart is classically associated with which lesion?
exam1.explanation: Left atrial isomerism (often with AV septal defect) and congenitally corrected transposition are the classic structural causes of fetal complete heart block. Isolated block with a normal heart is usually antibody mediated.
exam1.hint: Think of a heterotaxy syndrome in which the sinus node and conduction system are abnormal.

exam1.question: An intrapericardial heterogeneous mass with cystic components and a large pericardial effusion is most likely which tumor?
exam1.explanation: Intrapericardial teratomas are heterogeneous, often with cystic areas and calcification, and typically cause a large pericardial effusion. Rhabdomyomas are homogeneous and intramyocardial.
exam1.hint: Heterogeneous tissue types suggest a germ cell origin.

exam1.question: Which 3D/4D display shows multiple parallel slices of an acquired heart volume simultaneously, similar to CT or MRI?
exam1.explanation: Tomographic ultrasound imaging displays a series of parallel planes at selected intervals, allowing four-chamber, outflow and three-vessel planes to be shown together. Inversion mode renders fluid-filled structures as solid.
exam1.hint: The display resembles a stack of cross-sectional slices.

exam1.question: The bicaval view, showing the superior and inferior venae cavae entering the right atrium, is obtained in which plane?

options.text: Transverse plane at the level of the stomach
Left parasagittal plane through the ductal arch

exam1.explanation: The bicaval view is a right parasagittal (longitudinal) plane showing both cavae entering the right atrium. The ductal arch is seen in a more leftward sagittal plane.
exam1.hint: The venae cavae lie on the fetal right, so the probe is swept toward that side in a longitudinal orientation.

exam1.question: A mother is treated with indomethacin in the third trimester for preterm labor. Which fetal cardiovascular complication is the main concern?

options.text: Premature closure of the ductus venosus

exam1.explanation: NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, which maintains ductal patency, and can cause ductal constriction with high ductal velocities, tricuspid regurgitation and right ventricular dysfunction, especially after about 32 weeks.
exam1.hint: Recall which fetal shunt is kept open by prostaglandins.

exam1.question: The gooseneck deformity describes an elongated, narrowed left ventricular outflow tract seen in which lesion?
exam1.explanation: In AVSD the aortic valve is displaced anteriorly and the inlet is scooped, elongating and narrowing the LVOT into the classic gooseneck shape.
exam1.hint: Recall which defect changes the normal wedged position of the aortic valve between the AV valves.

exam1.question: Congenitally corrected transposition (L-TGA) is characterized by which combination?

options.text: Concordance at both levels with a large VSD

exam1.explanation: In ccTGA the ventricles are inverted (AV discordance) and the arteries are transposed (VA discordance), so blood flow is physiologically corrected. It is associated with complete heart block.
exam1.hint: Trace systemic venous blood from the right atrium to the lungs, and identify each ventricle by its morphology rather than its position.

exam1.question: In twin-twin transfusion syndrome, which cardiac complication is classically acquired by the recipient twin?
exam1.explanation: The volume-loaded, hypertensive recipient develops ventricular hypertrophy, AV valve regurgitation and acquired pulmonary stenosis or atresia. AVSD and TGA are developmental lesions, not acquired.
exam1.hint: The recipient experiences volume and pressure overload of the right heart.

exam1.question: A fetus has sustained sinus bradycardia of about 100 bpm with 1:1 AV conduction and a normal heart. Which condition should be considered?
exam1.explanation: Sustained mild sinus bradycardia with 1:1 conduction is a recognized presentation of congenital long QT syndrome, which may also show functional 2:1 block or ventricular tachycardia. WPW is associated with SVT rather than bradycardia.
exam1.hint: Persistent bradycardia with normal AV conduction in a normal heart can be the first sign of an inherited conduction disorder that a postnatal ECG would confirm.

exam1.question: A fetus has the abdominal aorta and IVC on the same side of the spine with the IVC anterior, plus a complex AVSD and anomalous pulmonary veins. Which heterotaxy syndrome is most likely?
exam1.explanation: Right isomerism shows juxtaposition of the aorta and IVC on the same side, complex lesions such as AVSD and total anomalous pulmonary venous return, and asplenia. Left isomerism features interrupted IVC with azygos continuation and heart block.
exam1.hint: Juxtaposed great vessels in the abdomen and anomalous venous return point to bilateral right-sidedness.

exam1.question: Per AIUM guidance, which thermal index should be monitored during a second-trimester fetal echocardiogram?

options.text: TIS, thermal index for soft tissue
TIC, thermal index for cranial bone

exam1.explanation: After about 10 weeks, when fetal bone begins to ossify, the bone thermal index is monitored. TIS applies earlier in pregnancy, and TIC applies to transcranial adult imaging.
exam1.hint: Fetal ossification is under way by the second trimester.

exam1.question: In a transverse view of the upper abdomen in a fetus with normal situs (situs solitus), where are the abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava located?

options.text: Aorta right of the spine; IVC left and anterior
Aorta left of the spine; IVC right and anterior to the aorta
Aorta and IVC side by side on the right of the spine
IVC directly posterior to the aorta on the left

exam1.explanation: In situs solitus the aorta lies to the left of the spine and the IVC lies to the right and slightly anterior, with the stomach on the left. Both vessels on the same side, or an IVC behind the aorta, raises concern for heterotaxy.
exam1.hint: Normal visceral situs places the stomach and the larger artery on the same side.

exam1.question: After birth, the ductus arteriosus becomes which structure?
exam1.explanation: The closed ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, the umbilical vein the ligamentum teres, and the foramen ovale the fossa ovalis.
exam1.hint: Match the remnant name to the arterial versus venous origin of the shunt.

exam1.question: A cleft in the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is most often associated with which defect?

options.text: Partial atrioventricular septal defect with primum ASD

exam1.explanation: A cleft left AV valve accompanies a primum ASD in partial AVSD; the left component of the AV valve is trileaflet rather than a true mitral valve.
exam1.hint: The cleft results from abnormal endocardial cushion development.

exam1.question: In congenitally corrected transposition, the left atrium connects to which ventricle?

options.text: Morphologic left ventricle, which gives rise to the aorta
Morphologic right ventricle, which gives rise to the pulmonary artery
Morphologic left ventricle, which gives rise to the pulmonary artery
Morphologic right ventricle, which gives rise to the aorta

exam1.explanation: In ccTGA the left atrium drains through the tricuspid valve into the left-sided morphologic right ventricle, identified by its moderator band, which ejects into the aorta. The morphologic right ventricle therefore serves as the systemic ventricle.
exam1.hint: Identify the left-sided ventricle by its moderator band and apically inserted AV valve.

exam1.question: In tricuspid atresia, how does systemic venous return leave the right atrium?

options.text: Through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle
Through the coronary sinus into the left ventricle
Across the foramen ovale to the left atrium
Retrograde into the superior vena cava

exam1.explanation: With no right AV connection, all systemic venous return must cross the atrial septum (an obligatory right-to-left shunt) to the left atrium and left ventricle. Blood reaches the small RV via a VSD.
exam1.hint: The right-sided AV valve has no opening.

exam1.question: Fetal hydrops is typically defined by abnormal fluid collection in how many body compartments?
exam1.explanation: Hydrops is defined as abnormal fluid in two or more compartments, such as ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion or skin edema. A single isolated collection is not hydrops.
exam1.hint: Isolated ascites alone does not meet the definition.

exam1.question: Which finding is characteristic of left atrial isomerism (polysplenia)?

options.text: Interrupted IVC with azygos continuation posterior to the aorta
Aorta and IVC juxtaposed anteriorly on the same side
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return in nearly all cases

exam1.explanation: Left isomerism typically has an interrupted infrahepatic IVC with azygos continuation, seen as a vessel beside or behind the aorta (double vessel sign), often with complete heart block. Juxtaposition and TAPVR suggest right isomerism.
exam1.hint: Look for an extra venous channel running alongside the descending aorta.

exam1.question: Which imaging mode generally delivers the highest time-averaged acoustic intensity to a small area of the fetus?
exam1.explanation: Pulsed Doppler concentrates energy on a stationary sample volume with high PRF, giving the highest time-averaged intensity; its use should be brief in keeping with ALARA. B-mode spreads energy across a scanned field.
exam1.hint: Intensity is greatest where a beam is held still and pulsed rapidly.

exam1.question: Which finding confirms that a great artery arising from a ventricle is the pulmonary artery?

options.text: It gives rise to the head and neck vessels
It arises from the posterior ventricle
It courses directly to the right of the trachea
It branches early into right and left branches

exam1.explanation: The main pulmonary artery is short and bifurcates soon after its origin into the right and left pulmonary arteries, continuing as the ductus. The aorta travels farther before branching and supplies the head and neck vessels.
exam1.hint: Follow the vessel a short distance and note where it divides.

exam1.question: Which component is part of the fetal cardiovascular profile score?

options.text: Venous Doppler of the umbilical vein and ductus venosus

exam1.explanation: The 10-point cardiovascular profile score assesses hydrops, venous Doppler, heart size, cardiac function and arterial (umbilical artery) Doppler. Breathing movements and fluid volume belong to the biophysical profile.
exam1.hint: Separate the cardiovascular profile from the biophysical profile.

exam1.question: A sinus venosus atrial septal defect near the superior vena cava entry is commonly associated with which anomaly?

options.text: Persistent left superior vena cava to coronary sinus
Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return of the right upper pulmonary vein

exam1.explanation: Superior sinus venosus defects are frequently associated with anomalous drainage of the right upper pulmonary vein into the SVC or right atrium. A cleft mitral valve accompanies primum defects.
exam1.hint: Consider which pulmonary vein lies immediately adjacent to the SVC-right atrial junction.

exam1.question: Which finding best distinguishes truncus arteriosus from tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia?

options.text: A VSD is present beneath the overriding vessel
The pulmonary arteries arise directly from the single arterial trunk
Only one semilunar valve is visible

exam1.explanation: In truncus arteriosus the pulmonary arteries arise from the common trunk itself, whereas in TOF with pulmonary atresia they are supplied by the ductus or collaterals. A VSD and a single visible outflow valve occur in both.
exam1.hint: Trace the origin of the branch pulmonary arteries.

exam1.question: What is typically seen on the four-chamber view in tricuspid atresia?

options.text: An echogenic plate in place of the tricuspid valve with a dominant left ventricle and small right ventricle
Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve with a large right atrium
A common AV valve with loss of offset
Two normal AV valves with a dilated right ventricle

exam1.explanation: Tricuspid atresia shows a dense fibrous plate at the right AV junction, no inflow on color Doppler, a small right ventricle and a dominant left ventricle, usually with a VSD. Apical displacement describes Ebstein anomaly.
exam1.hint: Apply color Doppler to the right AV junction and look for absent inflow.

exam1.question: In developed countries, most cases of fetal hydrops are of which type?
exam1.explanation: With widespread anti-D prophylaxis, about 90 percent of hydrops cases are nonimmune, with cardiovascular causes among the most common. Rh disease is now a minority cause.
exam1.hint: Consider the impact of routine Rh immune globulin.

exam1.question: Which first-trimester nuchal translucency measurement is the most widely taught threshold for referral for fetal echocardiography?
exam1.explanation: An NT of 3.5 mm or greater (above the 99th percentile) is the most widely used threshold for fetal echo, even with normal chromosomes; some centers use 3.0 mm. Lower values are within normal range.
exam1.hint: The threshold corresponds roughly to the 99th percentile.

exam1.question: The mechanical index displayed on the system primarily estimates the potential for which bioeffect?
exam1.explanation: The mechanical index relates to nonthermal effects such as cavitation and is based on peak rarefactional pressure and frequency. Tissue heating is estimated by the thermal index.
exam1.hint: The index is calculated from peak negative pressure.

exam1.question: A fetus has a large left congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The heart is displaced into the right chest but the apex still points to the left. What is the correct term for this cardiac position?
exam1.explanation: Dextroposition is a shift of the heart into the right chest from an extrinsic cause while the apex still points left. Dextrocardia means the base-to-apex axis itself points to the right.
exam1.hint: Separate where the heart sits from which way its apex points.

exam1.question: Using color Doppler, how is the ductus venosus best identified for spectral sampling?

options.text: As a narrow vessel with high-velocity aliasing flow at its inlet from the umbilical vein
As the largest vein entering the right atrium from below
As a low-velocity vessel posterior to the descending aorta
As the vessel passing directly through the portal sinus to the stomach

exam1.explanation: The ductus venosus is a narrow trumpet-shaped vessel whose inlet (isthmus) shows aliasing because of high velocity, making it the ideal sampling site. Sampling the nearby hepatic veins or IVC instead gives misleading waveforms.
exam1.hint: Velocity rises where the vessel is narrowest, and color shows this as a change in hue.

exam1.question: On the four-chamber view, a tubular structure is seen along the posterior left atrioventricular groove opening into the right atrium and mimicking a primum ASD. A fourth vessel is seen to the left of the pulmonary artery in the three-vessel view. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return to the portal vein
Interrupted inferior vena cava with azygos continuation
Persistent left superior vena cava draining to a dilated coronary sinus

exam1.explanation: A persistent left SVC drains into the coronary sinus, dilating it so it can mimic a primum ASD on a slightly caudal four-chamber view, and appears as an extra vessel left of the pulmonary artery. Azygos continuation produces an extra vessel beside the descending aorta instead.
exam1.hint: Count the vessels in the upper mediastinum and note where the extra one lies.

exam1.question: Which genetic condition is most strongly associated with truncus arteriosus?
exam1.explanation: Up to about 30 to 40 percent of truncus cases are associated with 22q11.2 deletion. Trisomy 21 is more associated with AV septal defects.
exam1.hint: Think of the microdeletion that is also associated with hypocalcemia and immune deficiency, for which a three-vessel-trachea view may prompt genetic testing.

exam1.question: What is the defining feature of Ebstein anomaly?

options.text: Apical displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets
Thickened tricuspid leaflets attached normally at the annulus

exam1.explanation: Ebstein anomaly involves apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets, creating an atrialized portion of the right ventricle and massive right atrial enlargement with tricuspid regurgitation. Normal annular attachment with thick leaflets describes tricuspid valve dysplasia.
exam1.hint: Compare the hinge points of the two AV valves on the septum.

exam1.question: In a fetus with worsening heart failure, pulsations appearing in the umbilical vein Doppler indicate what?

options.text: Normal physiologic variation in the third trimester

exam1.explanation: Umbilical venous pulsations reflect markedly elevated right atrial and central venous pressure transmitted through the ductus venosus, a late and ominous sign of heart failure.
exam1.hint: Pulsations travel backward from the heart when filling pressures are high.

exam1.question: Which type of twin pregnancy is an indication for fetal echocardiography?

options.text: Any twins with a male fetus

exam1.explanation: Monochorionic twins have a higher risk of congenital heart disease and of acquired cardiac changes from twin-twin transfusion syndrome. Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are not by themselves a standard indication.
exam1.hint: Shared placental circulation is the key risk factor.

exam1.question: Which fetal position generally provides the best transabdominal four-chamber view?

options.text: Spine posterior with the anterior chest facing the transducer
Spine directly anterior beneath the transducer
Fetus prone with the ribs and spine between the transducer and the heart
Any position, as shadowing does not affect the heart

exam1.explanation: With the spine posterior, the heart lies close to the transducer without rib or spine shadowing. A spine-anterior position causes acoustic shadowing that obscures cardiac structures.
exam1.hint: Bone between the transducer and the heart causes shadowing.

exam1.question: An echogenic intracardiac focus is most commonly located in which part of the fetal heart?

options.text: Moderator band of the right ventricle
Atrial septum near the foramen ovale
Papillary muscle of the left ventricle

exam1.explanation: Echogenic intracardiac foci are bright reflections usually located in the left ventricular papillary muscle (chordae). Isolated foci are generally regarded as a normal variant in low-risk pregnancies.
exam1.hint: The focus sits within the subvalvular apparatus of the systemic AV valve.

exam1.question: Beyond the first trimester, what is the normal Doppler appearance of the intra-abdominal umbilical vein?

options.text: Pulsatile flow with each atrial contraction

exam1.explanation: Normal umbilical venous flow is continuous and non-pulsatile after the first trimester. Pulsations transmitted from the heart indicate elevated central venous pressure, as in heart failure.
exam1.hint: Pulsations in this vessel mean pressure is being transmitted backward through the ductus venosus.

exam1.question: The flap of the foramen ovale is formed by which embryologic structure?
exam1.explanation: The thin mobile flap of the foramen ovale is the septum primum, which closes against the thicker septum secundum after birth. The endocardial cushions form the AV septum.
exam1.hint: The flap is the first, thinner septum to form.

exam1.question: In the Collett and Edwards classification of truncus arteriosus, type I is defined by which feature?

options.text: The branch pulmonary arteries arise separately from the posterior truncus
A short main pulmonary trunk arises from the truncus and then divides
The branch pulmonary arteries arise from the lateral walls of the truncus
Pulmonary blood flow comes only from aortopulmonary collaterals

exam1.explanation: Type I has a short main pulmonary segment arising from the truncus that divides into branch pulmonary arteries; types II and III have separate branch origins from the posterior and lateral walls. The former type IV is now considered pulmonary atresia with collaterals.
exam1.hint: The lowest type number has the most normal-looking pulmonary arterial branching.

exam1.question: Which finding best distinguishes tricuspid valve dysplasia from Ebstein anomaly?

options.text: The tricuspid leaflets are thickened but attached normally at the annulus

exam1.explanation: Both lesions can cause severe tricuspid regurgitation, right atrial enlargement and cardiomegaly. The distinguishing feature is the leaflet attachment point, which is normal in dysplasia and apically displaced in Ebstein anomaly.
exam1.hint: Most hemodynamic findings overlap, so focus on the anatomy of leaflet insertion.

exam1.question: How is the myocardial performance (Tei) index calculated?

options.text: Ejection time divided by isovolumic relaxation time
Peak E velocity divided by peak A velocity
End-diastolic minus end-systolic diameter, divided by end-diastolic diameter
Isovolumic contraction time plus isovolumic relaxation time, divided by ejection time

exam1.explanation: MPI equals (ICT + IRT) / ET and reflects combined systolic and diastolic function; a higher value indicates worse function. The diameter formula describes fractional shortening.
exam1.hint: The numerator combines the two periods when all valves are closed.

exam1.question: Which family history carries the higher recurrence risk of congenital heart disease in offspring?

options.text: A cousin with a bicuspid aortic valve

exam1.explanation: Offspring of affected mothers generally have a higher CHD recurrence risk than offspring of affected fathers, and first-degree relatives carry higher risk than distant relatives.
exam1.hint: Recurrence risk is consistently reported as higher with one parent.

exam1.question: According to widely used fetal cardiac screening guidelines, how much should the display be magnified?

options.text: The entire fetal trunk should fill the screen
The heart should fill about one-tenth of the screen
The heart should fill at least one-third to one-half of the screen
Zoom should not be used to avoid artifacts

exam1.explanation: Guidelines recommend zooming so the heart occupies at least a third to half of the display, improving spatial detail and frame rate. A whole-trunk view makes small defects hard to see.
exam1.hint: Magnification improves detail of small structures such as valves and septa.

exam1.question: At about 20 weeks of gestation, what is the expected relationship between right and left ventricular size on the four-chamber view?

options.text: Right ventricle about twice the left ventricle
Left ventricle about twice the right ventricle
Right ventricle about half the left ventricle

exam1.explanation: In midgestation the ventricles are nearly equal in width, with mild right-sided dominance becoming normal in the third trimester. Marked disproportion in midgestation suggests left or right heart obstruction such as coarctation.
exam1.hint: Mild right dominance is acceptable only later in pregnancy.

exam1.question: Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery most directly reflects which abnormality?

options.text: Reduced fetal blood viscosity from anemia

exam1.explanation: Loss of end-diastolic flow results from obliteration of placental villous vessels and high downstream resistance, typically in placental insufficiency. Anemia increases rather than decreases velocities.
exam1.hint: The umbilical artery waveform reflects the resistance of the vascular bed downstream.

exam1.question: Which approach most reliably confirms a suspected small ventricular septal defect prenatally?

options.text: A single apical view with high gain
Demonstrating the defect in two orthogonal planes with color Doppler flow across it

exam1.explanation: A true VSD should be seen in two planes, ideally with the beam perpendicular to the septum, and confirmed by color flow crossing the septum. A single apical view is prone to dropout artifact.
exam1.hint: An artifact rarely persists when the plane and angle of insonation change.

exam1.question: Double outlet right ventricle is commonly defined by which criterion?

options.text: Both great arteries arise entirely from the left ventricle
A single great artery overrides the septum
The aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left
More than 50 percent of both great arteries arise from the right ventricle

exam1.explanation: The widely used 50 percent rule defines DORV as more than half of each great artery committed to the right ventricle. Aorta from RV and pulmonary artery from LV describes transposition.
exam1.hint: The name describes how many outlets the right ventricle has.

exam1.question: In severe Ebstein anomaly, a circular shunt is identified by which combination of Doppler findings?

options.text: Antegrade pulmonary flow with a normal ductus
Left-to-right atrial flow with mitral stenosis
Pulmonary valve regurgitation with retrograde ductal flow and severe tricuspid regurgitation
Reversed umbilical artery diastolic flow only

exam1.explanation: In a circular shunt, blood flows from the aorta retrogradely through the ductus into the pulmonary artery, back across a regurgitant pulmonary valve into the RV, through the regurgitant tricuspid valve, and across the foramen ovale, bypassing the systemic circulation. This carries a very poor prognosis.
exam1.hint: Trace a loop of blood that returns to where it started without reaching the body.

exam1.question: When measuring ventricular fractional shortening by M-mode, how should the cursor be positioned?

options.text: Parallel to the septum through the apex
Perpendicular to the septum just below the AV valves
Through the atria above the AV valves
Through the aortic arch in the sagittal plane

exam1.explanation: The cursor should cross both ventricles perpendicular to the septum at the level just below the AV valve leaflets to measure end-diastolic and end-systolic dimensions. Oblique placement overestimates dimensions.
exam1.hint: Dimensions are accurate only when the beam crosses the walls at a right angle.

exam1.question: Which abdominal wall defect is more commonly associated with congenital heart disease?
exam1.explanation: Omphalocele is associated with cardiac defects in a substantial proportion of cases and with aneuploidy and syndromes such as Beckwith-Wiedemann. Gastroschisis is usually isolated.
exam1.hint: One defect is membrane-covered and frequently syndromic.

exam1.question: When applying color Doppler to the fetal heart, how should the color box size be chosen?

options.text: As small as needed to cover the region of interest
As large as possible to include the abdomen
Box size has no effect on frame rate

exam1.explanation: A larger color box requires more pulses per line and reduces frame rate, so the box should be limited to the area of interest. A small box preserves temporal resolution for fast fetal heart rates.
exam1.hint: Each color line requires multiple pulses, which costs time.

exam1.question: In the short-axis view at the base of the heart, which vessel appears as a circle in the center with the right ventricular outflow tract wrapping anteriorly around it?
exam1.explanation: In the basal short-axis view the aortic root is seen in cross section centrally while the RVOT and main pulmonary artery sweep around it anteriorly, the so-called circle and sausage. This confirms normal crossing of the great arteries.
exam1.hint: The outflow tract that wraps around is the sausage; the one in cross section is the circle.

exam1.question: Which inferior vena cava Doppler finding is considered normal in a second-trimester fetus?

options.text: Large reversal exceeding forward flow in each cycle
A small brief reversal of flow during atrial contraction
Continuous flow with no phasic variation

exam1.explanation: The fetal IVC normally shows a triphasic pattern with a small reversed a wave, and the percentage of reverse flow decreases with gestation. In contrast, a reversed a wave in the ductus venosus is abnormal.
exam1.hint: Compare the IVC with the ductus venosus, which normally stays above baseline.

exam1.question: The Rastelli classification is used to describe which lesion?
exam1.explanation: Rastelli types A, B and C describe the attachments and bridging of the superior leaflet of the common AV valve in complete AVSD. Truncus arteriosus is described by the Collett-Edwards or Van Praagh systems.
exam1.hint: The classification focuses on the anterior bridging leaflet of a common valve.

exam1.question: In double outlet right ventricle, what is the only outlet for the left ventricle?
