exam1.explanation: Because both great arteries arise from the right ventricle, left ventricular blood must cross the VSD to exit. The VSD location (subaortic, subpulmonary, doubly committed or remote) determines physiology and repair.
exam1.hint: Neither great artery is connected to the left-sided ventricle.

exam1.question: Immediately after birth, systemic circulation in hypoplastic left heart syndrome depends on which structure?
exam1.explanation: The right ventricle supplies the body through the ductus arteriosus, so prostaglandin infusion is needed to keep it open until staged palliation. Closure of the ductus causes shock.
exam1.hint: Identify which fetal shunt delivers right ventricular output to the descending aorta.

exam1.question: On M-mode, which finding characterizes a premature ventricular contraction?

options.text: An early atrial contraction followed by a normal ventricular beat
Regular atrial contractions with no ventricular response
A run of 1:1 beats at 250 bpm
An early ventricular contraction not preceded by an atrial contraction

exam1.explanation: A PVC appears as an early ventricular wall contraction without a preceding atrial contraction, often followed by a compensatory pause. An early atrial beat followed by a ventricular beat describes a conducted PAC.
exam1.hint: Note which chamber starts the premature beat.

exam1.question: On a transverse view of the normal fetal atria, how does the morphologic right atrial appendage differ from the left atrial appendage?

options.text: It is narrow and finger-like, while the left is broad and triangular
It is broad-based and triangular, while the left is narrow and finger-like
It receives the pulmonary veins, while the left appendage does not
It is a blind tubular pouch identical in shape to the left appendage

exam1.explanation: The morphologic right atrial appendage is broad-based and triangular, whereas the left atrial appendage is long, narrow and finger-like. Reversing these shapes is the common error; appendage morphology is the most reliable way to define atrial situs, which matters in heterotaxy.
exam1.hint: Think of the classic shape descriptions used to define atrial situs and isomerism.

exam1.question: The common atrioventricular valve in a complete atrioventricular septal defect typically has how many leaflets?

options.text: Two leaflets, resembling a normal mitral valve
Three leaflets, resembling a normal tricuspid valve
Five leaflets, including superior and inferior bridging leaflets
Four leaflets, with no bridging leaflets

exam1.explanation: The common valve in a complete AVSD usually has five leaflets: superior and inferior bridging leaflets that cross the septum plus three mural leaflets. The bridging leaflets explain why the AV valves lie at the same level and lose normal offset.
exam1.hint: Remember the leaflets that cross the defect from one ventricle to the other.

exam1.question: Which lesion is NOT classified as a conotruncal anomaly?
exam1.explanation: Conotruncal anomalies arise from abnormal development of the outflow tracts and great arteries and include tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, DORV, transposition and interrupted arch. Ebstein anomaly is a malformation of the tricuspid valve and inlet, not of the outflow tracts.
exam1.hint: Ask which lesion involves an inflow valve rather than the outflow tracts.

exam1.question: When evaluating a fetus for possible coarctation of the aorta, the carotid-subclavian artery index is calculated from which measurements?

options.text: Aortic isthmus velocity divided by ductus arteriosus velocity
Ascending aorta diameter divided by main pulmonary artery diameter
Transverse arch diameter divided by the distance between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries
Left ventricular length divided by right ventricular length

exam1.explanation: The carotid-subclavian artery index divides the transverse arch diameter at the left carotid by the distance between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries; a low index suggests coarctation because the arch is small and the segment elongated. Great artery and ventricular ratios support the suspicion but are not this index.
exam1.hint: The index uses two measurements taken from the same sagittal arch view.

exam1.question: A 25-year-old at 32 weeks has an irregular fetal rhythm caused by frequent premature atrial contractions. The heart is structurally normal, but a large, redundant foramen ovale flap billows deep into the left atrium. What is the significance of the flap?

options.text: It indicates a restrictive foramen ovale that requires early delivery
Redundant atrial septal tissue is associated with atrial ectopy that usually resolves
It is an early sign of evolving hypoplastic left heart syndrome
It indicates a high risk of immune-mediated complete heart block

exam1.explanation: An aneurysmal or redundant septum primum flap is a recognized association of fetal premature atrial contractions, which are usually benign and resolve. A redundant flap moving freely into the left atrium does not indicate restriction or left heart hypoplasia.
exam1.hint: Consider which benign arrhythmia is linked to atrial septal tissue touching the atrial wall.

exam1.question: According to AIUM fetal echocardiography guidance, which situation is an indication for fetal echocardiography because of an increased risk of congenital heart disease?

options.text: Pregnancy conceived by in vitro fertilization
Gestational hypertension in a previous pregnancy

exam1.explanation: Assisted reproductive technology, including in vitro fertilization, is associated with a modestly increased rate of congenital heart disease and is listed among indications for fetal echocardiography. A prior cesarean or treated hypothyroidism does not raise fetal cardiac risk enough to warrant a dedicated study.
exam1.hint: Consider which conception method is linked to a higher rate of CHD.

exam1.question: A sonographer switches from a 5 MHz to an 8 MHz transducer for an early fetal echocardiogram in a thin patient. Which trade-off results?

options.text: Better depth of penetration with reduced spatial resolution
Better spatial resolution with reduced depth of penetration
Higher frame rate with no change in spatial resolution
Less attenuation with increased acoustic shadowing

exam1.explanation: Higher frequency shortens the wavelength and pulse length, improving resolution, but attenuation increases so penetration decreases. That is why higher frequencies suit early gestation and thin patients, while lower frequencies are needed for deep imaging.
exam1.hint: Recall how attenuation changes with frequency.

exam1.question: In the normal three-vessel view at 22 weeks, which vessel has the largest diameter?
exam1.explanation: Normally the vessels decrease in size from fetal left to right: pulmonary artery larger than aorta, aorta larger than superior vena cava. The aorta is the tempting choice, but because the right ventricle ejects slightly more than half of the combined output, the pulmonary artery is the largest.
exam1.hint: Recall which ventricle is dominant in fetal life and which vessel it supplies.

exam1.question: Which property of the fetal myocardium makes fetal cardiac output depend heavily on heart rate rather than on increases in stroke volume?

options.text: Excess left ventricular preload delivered by the pulmonary veins
Very low systemic vascular resistance created by the placenta
Stiffer, less compliant myocardium with fewer organized contractile elements
Complete absence of autonomic innervation of the fetal heart

exam1.explanation: The immature fetal myocardium has a higher proportion of noncontractile tissue and is less compliant, so its ability to raise stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism is limited and output tracks heart rate. This is why sustained bradycardia or tachycardia is poorly tolerated; the low-resistance placenta affects afterload but is not the limiting factor.
exam1.hint: Consider why both very slow and very fast rhythms can lead to hydrops.

exam1.question: A 34-year-old at 23 weeks has a four-chamber view showing absence of the lower atrial septum at the crux, atrioventricular valves at the same level with two separate orifices, and a small inlet VSD with a narrow jet beneath the valves. Which lesion is most likely?

options.text: Complete atrioventricular septal defect with a common valve
Partial atrioventricular septal defect with an intact ventricular septum
Perimembranous VSD combined with a secundum atrial septal defect

exam1.explanation: A primum atrial defect with two separate AV valve orifices and a small, restrictive inlet ventricular component describes the intermediate (transitional) form. A complete AVSD has a single common orifice and a large inlet VSD, while a partial AVSD has no ventricular-level shunt.
exam1.hint: Combine the number of valve orifices with whether a ventricular-level shunt is present.

exam1.question: A 31-year-old at 24 weeks has a fetus with an intact ventricular septum. Color Doppler shows a direct communication between the ascending aorta and the main pulmonary artery just above two separate, normally formed semilunar valves. What is the diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: An aortopulmonary window is a communication between the ascending aorta and main pulmonary artery with two separate semilunar valves and usually an intact septum. Truncus arteriosus has a single semilunar (truncal) valve above a VSD, which is the key distinction.
exam1.hint: Count the semilunar valves and check the ventricular septum.

exam1.question: A 30-year-old at 28 weeks has a fetus with hypoplastic left heart syndrome. Which additional finding most worsens the prognosis for staged single-ventricle palliation?

options.text: Retrograde flow in the transverse aortic arch from the ductus
Moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation with reduced right ventricular function
Left-to-right flow across the foramen ovale
A small, slit-like left ventricle that does not form the apex

exam1.explanation: Because the right ventricle becomes the systemic ventricle, significant tricuspid regurgitation or right ventricular dysfunction is an adverse prognostic factor. Retrograde arch flow, left-to-right atrial flow and a hypoplastic left ventricle are expected features of HLHS rather than added risk.
exam1.hint: Ask which finding threatens the only ventricle the child will have.

exam1.question: Which M-mode or Doppler pattern characterizes Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree atrioventricular block?

options.text: A constant AV interval with sudden, unpredictable nonconducted atrial beats
Complete AV dissociation with an atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate
A premature atrial beat that is not conducted, followed by a pause
Progressive lengthening of the AV interval until an atrial beat is not conducted

exam1.explanation: In Mobitz type I block, the mechanical AV interval lengthens beat by beat until one atrial contraction fails to conduct, and the cycle then repeats. A constant AV interval with sudden dropped beats is Mobitz type II, and a blocked premature atrial beat is ectopy rather than AV block.
exam1.hint: Watch what happens to the AV interval in the beats before the dropped one.

exam1.question: A 26-year-old whose father has butterfly vertebrae and chronic cholestatic liver disease has a 22-week fetus with narrowing of the branch pulmonary arteries. Which syndrome is most likely?
exam1.explanation: Alagille syndrome (JAG1, autosomal dominant) causes peripheral or branch pulmonary artery stenosis along with bile duct paucity, butterfly vertebrae and characteristic facies. Williams syndrome can also cause branch pulmonary stenosis but is defined by supravalvular aortic stenosis and lacks the liver and vertebral findings.
exam1.hint: Link the parent's liver and spine findings to a dominant syndrome.

exam1.question: During a fetal echocardiogram, the heart looks laterally blurred and the transmit focal zone is set in the near field at the level of the maternal abdominal wall. What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Move the focal zone to the level of the fetal heart
Move the focal zone to the maximum image depth
Add focal zones in the near field to improve frame rate
Increase overall gain to sharpen the lateral borders

exam1.explanation: Lateral resolution is best at the focus, so a single focal zone should be placed at the level of the fetal heart. Adding focal zones lowers frame rate, and increasing gain brightens the image without improving resolution.
exam1.hint: Lateral resolution is best where the beam is narrowest.

exam1.question: A sonographer at 21 weeks examines the atrioventricular valves on a four-chamber view and notes that chordae from one valve attach directly to the ventricular septum. In a normal heart, which valve has these septal chordal attachments?

options.text: Neither valve, since both attach only to free-wall papillary muscles

exam1.explanation: The tricuspid valve has chordal attachments to the ventricular septum, a feature of the morphologic right ventricle. The mitral valve attaches to two papillary muscles on the free wall and does not attach to the smooth left ventricular septum.
exam1.hint: Septal attachments are one of the features used to identify the morphologic right ventricle.

exam1.question: Which factors are chiefly responsible for keeping the fetal ductus arteriosus open?

options.text: Circulating prostaglandin E2 and relatively low oxygen tension
High oxygen tension and circulating bradykinin
High pulmonary blood flow and low prostaglandin levels
Maternal estrogen and elevated fetal cortisol levels

exam1.explanation: Ductal patency in utero is maintained by prostaglandin E2 (largely of placental origin) and the low fetal oxygen tension. After birth, rising oxygen and falling prostaglandin levels cause constriction, which is also why maternal NSAIDs can constrict the fetal ductus.
exam1.hint: Consider why rising oxygen levels after birth and maternal NSAID use both narrow the duct.

exam1.question: A 29-year-old at 30 weeks has a fetus with a large, nonrestrictive perimembranous VSD and no cardiac failure. She asks when her baby might develop symptoms. When is heart failure from a large VSD typically expected?

options.text: At about 4 to 8 weeks of age as pulmonary vascular resistance falls
Within the first hours of life as the ductus arteriosus closes
Only after several years, when Eisenmenger physiology develops
Never, because large defects close spontaneously at birth

exam1.explanation: Left-to-right shunting across a large VSD increases as pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first weeks of life, so failure symptoms typically appear at about 4 to 8 weeks. Ductal closure does not drive VSD shunting, and Eisenmenger physiology is a late consequence of an unrepaired defect rather than the cause of early symptoms.
exam1.hint: Consider when the pressure difference driving the shunt becomes large after birth.

exam1.question: Which embryologic abnormality accounts for the features of tetralogy of Fallot?

options.text: Posterior deviation of the outlet septum into the left ventricle
Anterior and superior deviation of the outlet (conal) septum
Failure of fusion of the endocardial cushions
Complete failure of septation of the common arterial trunk

exam1.explanation: Anterosuperior deviation of the outlet septum narrows the right ventricular outflow, creates a malalignment VSD and causes the aorta to override; right ventricular hypertrophy follows postnatally. Posterior deviation instead narrows the subaortic region and is associated with interrupted aortic arch.
exam1.hint: Think about which way the septum shifts to narrow the pulmonary outflow.

exam1.question: Interrupted aortic arch type B occurs at which location?

options.text: Between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries
Distal to the left subclavian artery at the isthmus
Between the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries
Proximal to the origin of the brachiocephalic artery

exam1.explanation: Type B interruption, the most common form and strongly associated with 22q11.2 deletion, lies between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries. Type A is distal to the left subclavian artery, and type C is between the brachiocephalic and left carotid arteries.
exam1.hint: Types A, B and C move progressively proximal along the arch.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old at 26 weeks has a fetus with a persistent left superior vena cava and a dilated coronary sinus, and color Doppler shows flow passing from the coronary sinus directly into the left atrium through its roof. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: An unroofed coronary sinus is a deficiency of the wall between the coronary sinus and left atrium, often with a persistent left SVC, allowing interatrial communication through the sinus. A primum defect lies at the crux with loss of AV valve offset.
exam2.hint: The communication is through the wall separating a venous channel from the left atrium.

exam2.question: Which set of categories makes up the 10-point fetal cardiovascular profile score?

options.text: Heart rate, rhythm, axis, situs, and outflow tracts
Hydrops, venous Doppler, heart size, cardiac function, and arterial Doppler
Amniotic fluid, tone, movement, breathing, and heart rate
Nuchal fold, nasal bone, ductus venosus, tricuspid flow, and heart rate

exam2.explanation: The cardiovascular profile score assigns up to 2 points in each of five categories: hydrops, venous Doppler, heart size, cardiac function, and arterial (umbilical) Doppler; lower scores indicate worse heart failure. Amniotic fluid, tone, and breathing belong to the biophysical profile.
exam2.hint: This score was designed to grade fetal heart failure, so its categories reflect consequences of cardiac dysfunction rather than biophysical activity or aneuploidy markers.

exam2.question: How do fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas typically behave over time?

options.text: They may enlarge until the third trimester and usually regress after birth
They undergo malignant transformation in childhood
They calcify and enlarge steadily after birth
They always require surgical resection in the newborn

exam2.explanation: Rhabdomyomas often grow during gestation, peaking around the early third trimester, then usually regress spontaneously in infancy; surgery is reserved for obstruction or refractory arrhythmia. They are benign hamartomas.
exam2.hint: These hamartomas respond to the changing hormonal environment around birth.

exam2.question: At birth, what is the main reason the foramen ovale closes functionally?

options.text: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure
The ductus venosus constricts and raises right atrial pressure
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises with the first breath
Inferior vena cava return to the right atrium increases

exam2.explanation: Lung expansion lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and increases pulmonary venous return, raising left atrial pressure, while removal of the placenta lowers IVC return; the septum primum flap is pushed against septum secundum. Pulmonary resistance falls, not rises.
exam2.hint: Ask which atrium gains volume once the lungs open.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old at 32 weeks has a fetus whose right ventricle and pulmonary artery are larger than the left ventricle and aorta. The transverse arch and isthmus are small with a posterior shelf near the ductal insertion, and a persistent left SVC is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Ventricular and great artery disproportion favoring the right, a hypoplastic isthmus with a posterior shelf, and a left SVC are typical prenatal findings of coarctation. In HLHS the left ventricle is markedly hypoplastic with atresia of the left valves.
exam2.hint: Focus on the arch segment just before the ductal insertion.

exam2.question: A 36-year-old at 12 weeks 5 days has a nuchal translucency of 2.8 mm and ductus venosus Doppler showing a reversed a-wave. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Offer genetic testing and a detailed fetal echocardiogram
Reassure her because a reversed a-wave is normal before 14 weeks
Routine anatomy scan only since the NT is below 3.5 mm

exam2.explanation: A reversed a-wave in the first-trimester ductus venosus increases the risk of aneuploidy, congenital heart disease, and adverse outcome independent of NT thickness. Although some normal fetuses show it, the finding is not simply reassuring and should prompt further evaluation.
exam2.hint: In the first trimester, venous Doppler acts as a screening marker as well as a measure of cardiac loading.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old with low-risk cell-free DNA results has a 20-week scan showing a single focus within the left ventricular papillary muscle that is as bright as bone, with otherwise normal fetal anatomy and cardiac function. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: A normal variant with no added significance in this setting
A calcified rhabdomyoma suggesting tuberous sclerosis

exam2.explanation: An isolated echogenic intracardiac focus reflects papillary muscle mineralization and does not affect function; with a low-risk cell-free DNA result it carries no meaningful added risk. Rhabdomyomas are larger homogeneous masses within the myocardium, not a punctate bright focus.
exam2.hint: Consider what this bright focus represents histologically and how prior screening results change its significance.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old whose first child had hypoplastic left heart syndrome is now pregnant and asks when her fetal heart should be evaluated. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: A single fetal echo at 32 weeks
An optional early transvaginal scan at 12-14 weeks with a complete fetal echo at 18-22 weeks
Fetal echo only after 26 weeks, when structures are larger

exam2.explanation: Comprehensive fetal echocardiography is best performed at about 18-22 weeks; high-risk patients may have an early transvaginal study at 12-14 weeks, but it does not replace the mid-gestation exam because some lesions are too small or still evolving. Waiting until 32 weeks limits management options and image quality may worsen.
exam2.hint: Balance early reassurance with the timing that gives the most complete anatomic survey.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old at 22 weeks has a fetus with a defect in the posterior ventricular septum at the level of the AV valves, extending from beneath the tricuspid septal leaflet toward the crux, seen in the four-chamber view. AV valve offset is preserved and two separate valves are present. Which VSD type is this?
exam2.explanation: Inlet VSDs occupy the posterior septum beneath the AV valves and are seen in the four-chamber view; they can occur in isolation or as part of AVSD. Outlet defects are seen in the five-chamber or outflow views beneath the semilunar valves.
exam2.hint: The four-chamber plane shows the septal portion that separates the AV valve inflows.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old at 21 weeks has a four-chamber view in which slight posterior angulation shows an apparent opening in the lower atrial septum near the crux. The AV valves insert with normal offset, and returning to the true four-chamber plane shows an intact primum septum. What explains the finding?

options.text: A true ostium primum atrial septal defect
The normal coronary sinus mimicking an ostium primum defect

exam2.explanation: Angling posteriorly displays the coronary sinus running in the AV groove, which can mimic a primum ASD; preserved AV valve offset and an intact septum in the true four-chamber plane exclude a defect. A primum ASD lies at the crux with loss of offset.
exam2.hint: Note how the finding changed when the plane was corrected, and recall which normal structures lie just posterior to the four-chamber plane.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old at 20 weeks has a fetus with the stomach on the right, the heart in the right chest with the apex pointing right, the aorta to the right of the spine, and the IVC to the left. Cardiac connections appear otherwise normal. Which term describes this arrangement?
exam2.explanation: In situs inversus totalis every asymmetric organ is a mirror image of normal, including the heart (dextrocardia); the risk of CHD is low compared with heterotaxy. Isomerism produces discordant, symmetric arrangements such as the aorta and IVC on the same side.
exam2.hint: Check whether all organs are consistently mirrored or arranged discordantly.

exam2.question: Which STIC display mode shows multiple parallel slices through the volume simultaneously, similar to CT or MRI?
exam2.explanation: Tomographic ultrasound imaging displays a series of parallel planes at set intervals, allowing the four-chamber, outflow, and three-vessel views to be seen together. Inversion mode turns fluid-filled spaces into solid-appearing casts.
exam2.hint: Think of a display borrowed from cross-sectional imaging.

exam2.question: Which valve abnormality is most commonly associated with coarctation of the aorta?

options.text: Ebstein malformation of the tricuspid valve
Cleft of the anterior mitral leaflet

exam2.explanation: A bicuspid aortic valve is found in a large proportion of patients with coarctation, and both are common in Turner syndrome. A dysplastic pulmonary valve is typical of Noonan syndrome.
exam2.hint: Left-sided obstructive lesions tend to cluster.

exam2.question: A newborn with a prenatal diagnosis of pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum becomes cyanotic within hours of birth. Which medication should be started to maintain pulmonary blood flow?
exam2.explanation: With no antegrade pulmonary flow, the lungs are perfused through the ductus arteriosus, so prostaglandin E1 is given to keep it open. Indomethacin would promote ductal closure and worsen cyanosis.
exam2.hint: Pulmonary perfusion depends on keeping a fetal arterial channel open.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old at 34 weeks carries a fetus with HLHS. Pulmonary venous Doppler shows prominent reversed flow with atrial contraction and a low forward-to-reverse velocity-time integral ratio, and the atrial septum is thick with only a tiny color jet. What is the implication?

options.text: Restrictive atrial septum requiring immediate intervention at birth
An expected, benign finding in HLHS
Premature constriction of the ductus arteriosus

exam2.explanation: In HLHS all pulmonary venous return must exit the left atrium through the septum; a restrictive or intact septum causes left atrial hypertension with prominent pulmonary venous reversal, and these neonates need emergent septal decompression. The pulmonary venous pattern, not the tricuspid valve, reflects left atrial pressure.
exam2.hint: Pulmonary venous flow reflects how easily the left atrium can empty.

exam2.question: Which four-chamber view finding is most specific for an atrioventricular septal defect?

options.text: Septum primum flap moving into the left atrium
Right ventricle slightly larger than the left in late gestation
Loss of normal offset, with both AV valves inserting at the same level
Moderator band at the right ventricular apex

exam2.explanation: Normally the tricuspid valve inserts slightly more apically than the mitral; in AVSD a common junction causes linear insertion at the same level. Flap motion into the left atrium and mild late right ventricular dominance are normal.
exam2.hint: Compare where the two AV valves attach on the septum.

exam2.question: In a fetus with severe aortic stenosis, what does a brightly echogenic lining of the left ventricular cavity most likely represent?
exam2.explanation: Endocardial fibroelastosis is fibrous and elastic thickening of the endocardium from pressure overload and ischemia, appearing as a bright lining, and it impairs left ventricular function. The moderator band is a right ventricular structure.
exam2.hint: Think about the long-term effect of severe outflow obstruction on the left ventricular wall layers.

exam2.question: A 27-year-old at 22 weeks has a fetus with tetralogy of Fallot. Which serial measurement best predicts whether neonatal intervention will be needed soon after birth?

options.text: Pulmonary valve and branch pulmonary artery size with ductal flow direction
Size of the ventricular septal defect

exam2.explanation: Progressive pulmonary hypoplasia on serial Z-scores and reversal of ductal flow predict ductal-dependent pulmonary circulation and early intervention. The VSD in tetralogy is large and nonrestrictive, so its size adds little prognostic information.
exam2.hint: Focus on the degree of right outflow obstruction and how it evolves.

exam2.question: During which gestational window is surveillance for fetal AV block most important in a pregnancy with maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies?
exam2.explanation: Immune-mediated block usually develops between about 18 and 24 weeks, when maternal antibodies cross the placenta and injure the developing conduction system; weekly or biweekly PR monitoring is commonly performed from about 16 to 26 weeks. Onset after 30 weeks is uncommon.
exam2.hint: Antibody-mediated injury coincides with mid-gestation conduction system maturation.

exam2.question: A couple asks about the risk of CHD in their fetus. Which family history generally carries the highest recurrence risk?

options.text: The father has a congenital heart defect
One prior sibling had a congenital heart defect
A maternal first cousin had a congenital heart defect
The mother has a congenital heart defect

exam2.explanation: Recurrence is generally higher when the mother is affected (often cited around 3-7 percent, higher for some lesions such as AVSD) than when the father or a single sibling is affected (about 2-3 percent). Second- and third-degree relatives add little risk.
exam2.hint: Recurrence risk differs by which first-degree relative is affected.

exam2.question: Which statement about fetal combined ventricular output is accurate?

options.text: The right ventricle ejects somewhat more than half of the combined output
The left ventricle ejects about two-thirds of the combined output
Each ventricle ejects exactly half of the combined output
The ventricles pump in series as they do after birth

exam2.explanation: In the parallel fetal circulation the right ventricle ejects roughly 55-60 percent of combined output, receiving SVC return, coronary sinus return, and part of IVC flow. The series arrangement only develops after birth.
exam2.hint: Consider how much venous return streams to the right heart in fetal life.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old at 22 weeks has a fetus with a slit-like left ventricle that does not form the apex, no flow across the mitral valve, a 2-mm ascending aorta, retrograde flow in the transverse arch from the ductus, and left-to-right flow across the foramen ovale. What is the diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Mitral and aortic atresia with a diminutive left ventricle and ascending aorta, retrograde arch perfusion from the ductus, and reversed atrial shunting define HLHS. Coarctation has antegrade arch flow and a left ventricle that reaches the apex.
exam2.hint: Note the direction of flow in the transverse arch and across the atrial septum.

exam2.question: In an apical four-chamber view with the ultrasound beam parallel to the interventricular septum, the upper septum appears to have a gap. How should a VSD be confirmed or excluded?

options.text: Reimage from a subcostal or lateral approach with the beam perpendicular to the septum
Increase the overall gain until the gap fills in
Switch to a lower-frequency transducer in the same plane

exam2.explanation: Thin membranous septum parallel to the beam produces echo dropout that mimics a VSD; insonating perpendicular to the septum, with low-velocity color, confirms whether a defect is real. Raising gain adds noise and can mask a true defect.
exam2.hint: Specular reflectors return the strongest echoes when struck at a right angle.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old at 22 weeks has a fetus with tetralogy of Fallot and a right aortic arch, and the thymus appears small in the three-vessel-trachea view. Which test is most appropriate next?

options.text: Karyotype analysis limited to monosomy X
Chromosomal microarray to detect a 22q11.2 deletion

exam2.explanation: Conotruncal anomalies with a right aortic arch and thymic hypoplasia strongly suggest 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, best detected by microarray or FISH. A standard karyotype focused on monosomy X would miss this microdeletion.
exam2.hint: Recall the syndrome that links conotruncal anomalies, arch abnormalities, and thymic hypoplasia, then pick the test able to detect it.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old at 24 weeks has a fetus with a large heterogeneous mass containing cystic and solid components within the pericardium beside the right heart and great vessels, accompanied by a large pericardial effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Intrapericardial teratomas are heterogeneous, partly cystic masses usually attached to the great vessels and are characteristically associated with large pericardial effusions that can cause tamponade and hydrops. Rhabdomyomas are homogeneous intramyocardial masses.
exam2.hint: Combine the heterogeneous texture with the location outside the myocardium.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old with Sjogren syndrome has a 24-week fetus with isolated immune-mediated complete heart block and an atrial rate of 140 bpm. Which finding most worsens the prognosis?
exam2.explanation: Ventricular rates below about 55 bpm, hydrops, endocardial fibroelastosis, and ventricular dysfunction predict poor outcome in fetal complete heart block; beta-agonists may be used to raise the rate. A normal atrial rate is expected.
exam2.hint: Consider which parameters are used to decide when fetal complete heart block needs treatment.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old at 18 weeks has a fetus whose heart lies partly outside the chest through a distal sternal defect, with an upper abdominal omphalocele and an anterior diaphragmatic defect. What is the diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Pentalogy of Cantrell combines a midline supraumbilical abdominal wall defect, lower sternal defect, anterior diaphragmatic and diaphragmatic pericardial defects, and intracardiac anomalies, often with ectopia cordis. Body stalk anomaly involves a large defect with a very short or absent cord and scoliosis.
exam2.hint: Classify the defects as midline ventral wall closure abnormalities and recall the syndrome that combines them with ectopia cordis.

exam2.question: During sagittal sweeps of a 26-week fetus, the sonographer obtains a tightly curved arch that arises centrally in the chest and gives off three vessels from its superior aspect toward the neck. Which structure is displayed?
exam2.explanation: The aortic arch has a tight candy-cane curve and gives rise to the brachiocephalic, left carotid, and left subclavian arteries. The ductal arch is broader and flatter (hockey-stick shape), arises more anteriorly from the pulmonary trunk, and has no head and neck branches.
exam2.hint: Only one of the two fetal arches sends branches to the head and arms.

exam2.question: A 23-year-old who emigrated without childhood vaccinations had confirmed rubella at 8 weeks. Which cardiovascular findings are most characteristic of congenital rubella?

options.text: Hypoplastic left heart and restrictive atrial septum
Tetralogy of Fallot with absent pulmonary valve
Patent ductus arteriosus and branch pulmonary artery stenosis

exam2.explanation: Congenital rubella syndrome typically causes patent ductus arteriosus and peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, together with cataracts, deafness, and growth restriction. Absent pulmonary valve tetralogy is associated with 22q11.2 deletion.
exam2.hint: The classic triad of this infection includes eye, ear, and heart findings.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old at 23 weeks has a fetal echo showing a 1.5-mm hypoechoic rim confined to the region of the atrioventricular groove. There is no fluid elsewhere and cardiac function is normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: A significant effusion indicating early hydrops
A small amount of pericardial fluid within normal limits

exam2.explanation: A thin rim of pericardial fluid under about 2 mm, especially near the AV groove, is a common normal finding. Effusions thicker than about 2 mm, surrounding the heart, or accompanied by other fluid collections warrant evaluation for hydrops.
exam2.hint: Thickness and distribution are what separate physiologic pericardial fluid from a true effusion.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old at 23 weeks has a scan showing stomach and bowel loops in the left hemithorax at the four-chamber level. The heart lies in the right chest, but its apex still points to the left. Which term best describes the cardiac position?
exam2.explanation: Dextroposition is a shift of the whole heart into the right chest by an extracardiac process, here a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia, while the base-to-apex axis still points left. Dextrocardia means the base-to-apex axis itself points to the right.
exam2.hint: Separate a heart that has been pushed aside from one whose base-to-apex axis is itself reversed.

exam2.question: A 27-year-old at 24 weeks is referred after the three-vessel-trachea view showed the transverse aortic arch passing to the right of the trachea while the ductus arteriosus passes to the left, the two vessels joining behind the trachea in a U shape. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Left aortic arch with an aberrant right subclavian artery
Normal left aortic arch with a left ductus
Right aortic arch with a left ductus forming a vascular ring

exam2.explanation: Normally the aortic and ductal arches both lie left of the trachea and meet in a V. A right arch with a left ductus encircles the trachea and esophagus in a U-shaped vascular ring; if CHD is present, 22q11.2 deletion should be considered.
exam2.hint: Compare the side of the trachea each arch travels on with the normal V configuration.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old at 24 weeks has a structurally normal fetal heart with a rate of 145 bpm. Pulsed Doppler of mitral inflow shows an E-wave smaller than the A-wave. What is the best interpretation?
exam2.explanation: Fetal ventricles are relatively noncompliant and rely on atrial contraction, so an E/A ratio below 1 is normal and rises gradually toward term. Mitral stenosis would show high velocity with turbulence and a small LV.
exam2.hint: Fetal myocardium is relatively stiff, so atrial contraction contributes more to filling.

exam2.question: During a 24-week fetal echo with spectral Doppler, the beam passes through ossified fetal bone near the focal zone. Which output index should be monitored?
exam2.explanation: After about 10 weeks, when fetal bone is ossifying and may lie at the focus, TIb is the relevant index for obstetric scanning; TIs is used in early pregnancy and TIc is for transcranial adult imaging. MI relates to cavitation, which is of little concern in fetal tissue without gas.
exam2.hint: Heating is greatest where bone absorbs energy at the focus.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old at 26 weeks has a fetus with double outlet right ventricle in which the VSD lies beneath the pulmonary valve and the aorta is anterior and rightward. Which physiology does this arrangement resemble after birth?
exam2.explanation: In the Taussig-Bing form of DORV the subpulmonary VSD directs left ventricular blood into the pulmonary artery and right ventricular blood into the aorta, creating transposition physiology with cyanosis. A subaortic VSD produces VSD-like or tetralogy-like physiology instead.
exam2.hint: Follow where left ventricular blood goes through a subpulmonary defect.

exam2.question: In the three-vessel view of a normal fetus, which arrangement is expected from fetal left to right?

options.text: Aorta, pulmonary artery, superior vena cava, with the aorta largest
Superior vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery, with equal diameters
Pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava, with diameters decreasing in that order
Pulmonary artery, superior vena cava, aorta, with the aorta smallest

exam2.explanation: The normal three-vessel view shows the pulmonary artery on the left and most anterior, the aorta in the middle, and the SVC on the right and most posterior, decreasing in size. A larger aorta than pulmonary artery suggests right outflow obstruction such as tetralogy.
exam2.hint: Picture the outflow tracts sweeping from the anterior right ventricle toward the posterior systemic vein in the upper mediastinum.

exam2.question: A 27-year-old of East Asian descent at 23 weeks has a fetus with a VSD lying directly beneath both semilunar valves, with no muscular tissue separating the aortic and pulmonary valves. Which VSD type is this?
exam2.explanation: Doubly committed (subarterial, supracristal) VSDs result from absence of the conal septum and are more common in Asian populations; aortic cusp prolapse and regurgitation can develop. Perimembranous defects are bordered by the membranous septum near the tricuspid valve.
exam2.hint: Notice what is missing between the two semilunar valves.

exam2.question: A sonographer is about to document situs solitus in a 20-week fetus. Which step must be completed first?

options.text: Establish fetal left and right from the presentation and spine position
Measure the cardiac axis in the four-chamber view
Locate the gallbladder relative to the umbilical vein
Identify the side of the aortic arch relative to the trachea

exam2.explanation: Situs can only be assigned once the fetal left side is known, which is determined from fetal lie, presentation, and spine orientation; the stomach, aorta, IVC, and cardiac apex are then compared with that side. Measuring the axis first is meaningless if left and right are uncertain.
exam2.hint: You cannot call an organ left-sided until you know which side of the fetus is left.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old at 23 weeks has a fetal echo showing color flow in the ductus arteriosus directed from the aorta toward the pulmonary arteries throughout the cardiac cycle. What does this indicate?

options.text: Ductal-dependent systemic circulation from left heart obstruction
Ductal-dependent pulmonary circulation from severe right outflow obstruction
Premature constriction of the ductus arteriosus

exam2.explanation: Normal fetal ductal flow runs from the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta. Reversed (aorta-to-pulmonary) ductal flow means the lungs are supplied retrograde, as in pulmonary atresia or critical stenosis, and prostaglandin will be needed at birth.
exam2.hint: Determine which circulation the ductus is supplying when flow runs backward.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old at 30 weeks has a fetal bicaval view showing deficiency of the atrial wall at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, with the right upper pulmonary vein appearing to drain near that site. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Superior sinus venosus defect with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return

exam2.explanation: Superior sinus venosus defects lie at the SVC-right atrial junction, outside the true fossa ovalis, and are typically associated with anomalous drainage of the right upper pulmonary vein. Primum defects lie at the crux.
exam2.hint: Note the location of the deficiency relative to the fossa ovalis and caval entry.

exam2.question: To document the atrioventricular relationship in a fetus with an irregular rhythm using M-mode, where should the cursor be placed?

options.text: Through the ductus arteriosus in the three-vessel view
Through both ventricles only, below the AV valves
Through an atrial wall and a ventricular wall at the same time

exam2.explanation: M-mode rhythm analysis requires the cursor to cross an atrial wall and a ventricular wall (or an AV valve and a semilunar valve) simultaneously so the timing of atrial and ventricular contractions can be compared. A cursor through the ventricles alone cannot show atrial activity.
exam2.hint: You need to see both chambers' contractions on the same trace.

exam2.question: A 33-week fetus with hypoplastic left heart syndrome undergoes maternal hyperoxygenation testing. Which response suggests adequate pulmonary vascular reactivity and a less restrictive atrial septum?

options.text: No change in branch pulmonary artery PI
A rise in umbilical artery PI
Increased branch pulmonary artery flow with a fall in pulmonary artery PI
Reversal of the ductus venosus a-wave

exam2.explanation: Oxygen dilates the pulmonary vascular bed; a significant fall in branch pulmonary artery PI indicates reactive vessels, whereas a lack of response predicts a restrictive atrial septum needing urgent intervention after birth. An unchanged PI is the worrisome result.
exam2.hint: Consider what a reactive pulmonary vascular bed should do when maternal oxygen is given, and which vessel's index reflects it.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old at 26 weeks has a fetus with several cardiac rhabdomyomas. Which additional evaluation is most valuable for counseling?

options.text: Fetal brain MRI and genetic testing for TSC1 and TSC2
Repeat fetal echo only at 40 weeks

exam2.explanation: Because multiple rhabdomyomas strongly suggest tuberous sclerosis, fetal MRI to look for cortical tubers and subependymal nodules and TSC1/TSC2 testing guide prognosis, which depends mainly on neurologic involvement. Anti-Ro testing addresses heart block, not tumors.
exam2.hint: Multiple tumors of this type suggest an underlying genetic syndrome; consider where its most prognostically important lesions occur.

exam2.question: Which imaging mode typically delivers the highest time-averaged acoustic intensity and should therefore be used as briefly as possible during fetal echocardiography?
exam2.explanation: Pulsed-wave Doppler concentrates repeated pulses along a single line at a fixed gate, producing the highest time-averaged intensities and thermal indices; ALARA calls for limiting dwell time, especially in early pregnancy. B-mode spreads energy across a scanned field.
exam2.hint: Energy repeatedly delivered to one stationary spot causes the most heating.

exam2.question: In a normal 22-week fetus, an apparent aortic override seen in a five-chamber view obtained with the beam parallel to the septum disappears when the heart is imaged from a lateral approach. What explains the finding?

options.text: Spontaneous closure of a malalignment VSD

exam2.explanation: When the beam runs parallel to the septum, the thin membranous region and the aortic root can appear discontinuous, mimicking override; imaging perpendicular to the septum confirms septal-aortic continuity. A true malalignment VSD persists in every plane.
exam2.hint: Consider how the thin membranous septum and aortic root reflect when the beam runs parallel versus perpendicular to them.

exam2.question: A 30-week growth-restricted fetus with absent umbilical artery end-diastolic flow shows retrograde diastolic flow in the aortic isthmus. What does this finding represent?

options.text: Advanced redistribution with placental resistance exceeding cerebral resistance

exam2.explanation: The aortic isthmus links the left-ventricle-supplied brain circulation and the right-ventricle-supplied lower body and placenta; diastolic reversal means brain resistance has fallen below placental resistance, so blood flows back toward the head. It marks advanced hemodynamic compromise, not an anatomic narrowing.
exam2.hint: Flow direction in this segment reflects the relative downstream resistances of two parallel circuits.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old with bipolar disorder took lithium throughout the first trimester. Which cardiac lesion has been classically associated with this exposure?
exam2.explanation: First-trimester lithium has classically been linked to Ebstein anomaly, though modern data suggest the absolute risk is lower than originally reported; fetal echocardiography is still recommended. Truncus arteriosus is linked to 22q11.2 deletion.
exam2.hint: Recall the classic teratogen associations of psychiatric medications taken during organogenesis.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old at 28 weeks has a fetal cardiac area measuring 0.55 of the thoracic area at the four-chamber level, with normal-appearing chest size. How should this ratio be interpreted?

options.text: Normal heart size for this gestational age
A small heart relative to the thorax
Cardiomegaly that warrants a search for an underlying cause
A borderline value needing no further evaluation

exam2.explanation: The normal fetal heart fills about one-quarter to one-third of the thoracic area (cardiothoracic area ratio roughly 0.25-0.35), so 0.55 indicates cardiomegaly. Causes include tricuspid regurgitation, anemia, arteriovenous shunts, and cardiomyopathy.
exam2.hint: Recall what fraction of the chest a normal fetal heart occupies by area.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old at 24 weeks has a fetus with an AVSD whose common valve is committed mainly to the right ventricle, while the left ventricle is small and does not reach the apex. What is the most important implication?

options.text: Possible need for single-ventricle palliation instead of biventricular repair

exam2.explanation: An unbalanced AVSD with a hypoplastic left ventricle may not support a two-ventricle repair, so the degree of imbalance guides counseling toward single-ventricle palliation. AVSDs do not close spontaneously.
exam2.hint: Think about whether both ventricles can each support a circulation after surgery.

exam2.question: In a normal five-chamber (left ventricular outflow tract) view, which anatomic relationship is expected?

options.text: Aorta arising anteriorly from the right ventricle parallel to the pulmonary artery
Septum continuous with the anterior aortic wall and mitral leaflet continuous with the posterior aortic wall
Aorta overriding a defect in the outlet portion of the septum
Muscular conus separating the aortic valve from the mitral valve

exam2.explanation: Normal septal-aortic continuity and mitral-aortic fibrous continuity are confirmed in the five-chamber view. A subaortic muscular conus separating the aortic and mitral valves is characteristic of DORV and transposition, not normal anatomy.
exam2.hint: Look at what the anterior and posterior walls of the aortic root connect to.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old G2P1 at 21 weeks has a four-chamber view showing a normally sized heart in the left chest with the cardiac axis measured at 72 degrees to the left of midline. Which group of anomalies should prompt the most careful evaluation next?

options.text: Conotruncal anomalies such as tetralogy of Fallot
Systemic venous anomalies such as interrupted IVC

exam2.explanation: The normal axis is about 45 degrees (plus or minus about 20); marked left axis deviation is strongly associated with conotruncal lesions such as tetralogy of Fallot, truncus, and DORV, even when the four chambers look normal. Secundum ASDs do not shift the axis and cannot be diagnosed prenatally anyway.
exam2.hint: Compare the measured axis with the normal range and recall which lesion group most often shifts it.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old at 29 weeks has a fetus with sustained supraventricular tachycardia at 230 bpm and ascites, pleural effusions, and skin edema. Which transplacental therapy is generally preferred first?
exam2.explanation: In hydrops, placental transfer of digoxin is poor, so flecainide or sotalol (sometimes combined with digoxin) is generally favored; digoxin is often first-line only in the non-hydropic fetus. Terbutaline is used to raise the rate in heart block.
exam2.hint: Hydrops impairs placental transfer of one traditional drug.

exam2.question: A 30-week fetus with pulmonary stenosis has a jet that aliases with pulsed-wave Doppler even at the maximum scale. Which method best measures the peak velocity?
exam2.explanation: Continuous-wave Doppler has no Nyquist limit and can record high-velocity jets without aliasing, although it lacks range resolution. Higher transducer frequencies and lower scales make aliasing worse.
exam2.hint: Aliasing comes from limited pulse repetition frequency.

exam2.question: A 24-week fetus of a 34-year-old has critical aortic stenosis with a severely depressed left ventricular ejection, and the peak velocity across the valve is only 1.8 m/s. Why is this velocity misleading?

options.text: Reduced ventricular output lowers the gradient and underestimates severity
The jet is always overestimated in the fetus
Aortic velocity cannot be measured before 30 weeks
Low velocity proves the stenosis is mild

exam2.explanation: Doppler gradients depend on flow; a failing left ventricle with low output produces a deceptively low jet velocity even with a critically narrowed valve. Ventricular function and flow reversals must be considered along with velocity.
exam2.hint: Pressure gradient depends on both orifice size and the flow pushed through it.

exam2.question: A 24-year-old at 32 weeks returns for follow-up of a perimembranous VSD. A thin pouch of tissue from the tricuspid septal leaflet now bulges into the right ventricle and partly covers the defect, with reduced shunt flow. What is the significance?

options.text: A ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
Aneurysmal tissue that promotes partial or complete spontaneous closure

exam2.explanation: Accessory tricuspid tissue forming a membranous septal aneurysm is a common mechanism of spontaneous perimembranous VSD closure. Ebstein anomaly involves apical displacement of the septal leaflet hinge, not a pouch over a VSD.
exam2.hint: Consider the usual natural history of perimembranous defects and what tissue bulging over the defect means for it.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old at 25 weeks is evaluated for suspected congenitally corrected transposition. The left-sided ventricle contains a coarse apical muscle band, and its atrioventricular valve inserts on the septum closer to the apex than the opposite valve. How should the left-sided ventricle be classified?
exam2.explanation: The moderator band, coarse trabeculations, and the more apical septal insertion of its AV valve (the tricuspid) identify a morphologic right ventricle regardless of where it sits. In corrected transposition the morphologic RV is left-sided.
exam2.hint: Ventricular identity comes from internal features, not from which side of the chest the chamber occupies.

exam2.question: A 33-year-old at 21 weeks has a fetus with an echogenic band of tissue in place of the right AV valve, no flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle, a small right ventricle filled through a VSD, and all systemic venous return crossing the foramen ovale. What is the diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: In tricuspid atresia there is no right AV connection, so systemic venous return must cross the atrial septum to the left heart, and the hypoplastic right ventricle fills through a VSD. In pulmonary atresia with intact septum the tricuspid valve is patent but often small.
exam2.hint: Determine whether any inflow connection exists between the right atrium and right ventricle.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old with a BMI of 45 at 20 weeks has poor visualization of the fetal heart. Which approach is most helpful?

options.text: A lower-frequency transducer with tissue harmonics, scanning through thinner windows such as the periumbilical area
A high-frequency linear transducer to improve resolution
Increased persistence and a wider sector
Postponing the entire exam until 34 weeks

exam2.explanation: Lower frequencies penetrate thick tissue, harmonics reduce clutter, and windows such as the umbilicus or below the pannus shorten the path; repeat imaging at about 22-24 weeks may also help. Higher-frequency transducers penetrate less.
exam2.hint: Trade some resolution for penetration and shorten the tissue path.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old with Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy still has high thyroid-stimulating antibodies. At 30 weeks the fetal heart rate is 180-190 bpm with 1:1 conduction, normal variability, gradual rate changes, and a fetal goiter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Maternal stimulating antibodies can cross the placenta even after thyroidectomy, causing fetal thyrotoxicosis with goiter and sinus tachycardia, which shows variability and gradual changes and rarely exceeds about 200 bpm. Reentrant SVT is fixed, faster, and starts abruptly.
exam2.hint: Compare the rate, variability, and onset pattern with reentrant tachycardias, and consider the maternal history.

exam2.question: A 38-year-old with chronic hypertension has a 29-week fetus with an estimated weight under the 3rd percentile. Doppler of the umbilical artery shows flow reversal in diastole. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Severe placental insufficiency with markedly increased placental resistance
A normal waveform for this gestational age
Premature constriction of the ductus arteriosus

exam2.explanation: Reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery reflects severe obliteration of the placental vascular bed and is associated with high perinatal risk, prompting intensive surveillance and delivery planning. Anemia raises MCA velocity rather than reversing umbilical diastolic flow.
exam2.hint: Diastolic flow toward the placenta depends on how low its downstream resistance is.

exam2.question: A 30-week fetus with severe Ebstein anomaly has pulmonary valve regurgitation and retrograde flow in the ductus arteriosus. Which best describes this circulation?

options.text: A circular shunt in which blood loops through the ductus, right heart, atrial septum, and left heart
A favorable pattern indicating a competent pulmonary valve
Isolated ductal constriction from right heart failure
A normal fetal pattern in right heart disease

exam2.explanation: In a circular shunt, aortic blood runs retrograde through the ductus, regurgitates through the pulmonary and tricuspid valves, crosses the foramen ovale, and returns to the left heart, so systemic output is wasted; it carries a very poor prognosis. Ductal reversal with a competent pulmonary valve is far better tolerated.
exam2.hint: Follow a blood cell from the aorta and see whether it ever reaches the body.

exam2.question: In a normal 22-week fetus, how do the great arteries relate to each other as they leave the ventricles?

options.text: They run parallel, with the aorta anterior and to the right
They cross, with the pulmonary artery arising anteriorly and passing leftward over the aorta
They arise side by side from the right ventricle
They share a single valve before dividing into two vessels

exam2.explanation: Normally the pulmonary artery leaves the anterior right ventricle and crosses the aorta, which leaves the posterior left ventricle, producing a criss-cross relationship. Parallel great arteries suggest transposition or DORV.
exam2.hint: Picture where each ventricle sits and the direction each outflow tract takes as it leaves the heart.

exam2.question: A 24-year-old at 30 weeks has an irregular fetal rhythm caused by frequent conducted premature atrial contractions. The heart is structurally normal and there is no hydrops. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance with periodic heart-rate checks to detect tachycardia

exam2.explanation: Isolated PACs are the most common fetal arrhythmia and are usually benign, resolving spontaneously; a small percentage progress to SVT, so periodic heart-rate monitoring is advised. Antiarrhythmic drugs are reserved for sustained tachycardia.
exam2.hint: Recall the most common fetal arrhythmia and when antiarrhythmic therapy is actually indicated.

exam2.question: When differentiating double outlet right ventricle from tetralogy of Fallot with marked aortic override, which finding favors DORV?

options.text: Loss of fibrous continuity between the aortic and mitral valves

exam2.explanation: In tetralogy the aortic valve retains fibrous continuity with the mitral valve, whereas in DORV a subaortic conus separates them. A small pulmonary artery, malalignment VSD, and right arch can occur in both.
exam2.hint: Look at what lies between the aortic valve and the anterior mitral leaflet.

exam2.question: A 37-year-old at 20 weeks has a fetus with an absent nasal bone, a thickened nuchal fold, and short femurs. Which cardiac defect is most characteristic of the suspected condition?
exam2.explanation: These markers suggest trisomy 21, in which AVSD is the most characteristic cardiac lesion, along with VSD and tetralogy. Coarctation and HLHS are more typical of Turner syndrome.
exam2.hint: Match the soft markers to an aneuploidy, then recall its signature heart lesion.

exam2.question: In a fetus with severe tricuspid regurgitation and right atrial enlargement, which finding distinguishes tricuspid valve dysplasia from Ebstein anomaly?

options.text: The degree of right atrial enlargement
Normal annular attachment of the septal leaflet

exam2.explanation: Both lesions cause regurgitation, atrial dilation, and cardiomegaly; Ebstein anomaly is defined by apical displacement of the septal leaflet, whereas in dysplasia thickened leaflets hinge at the normal level. Severity measures cannot separate them.
exam2.hint: Recall which structural finding defines Ebstein anomaly.

exam2.question: A 27-year-old at 24 weeks has a fetus whose left atrium connects to a left-sided ventricle containing a moderator band, and that ventricle gives rise to the aorta. The atrial rate is 140 bpm and the ventricular rate is 58 bpm with no consistent relationship. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Double outlet right ventricle with blocked atrial bigeminy
Tetralogy of Fallot with second-degree block
Congenitally corrected transposition with complete heart block

exam2.explanation: Atrioventricular plus ventriculoarterial discordance defines congenitally corrected (L-) transposition; its displaced conduction system predisposes to complete heart block, and associated VSD, pulmonary stenosis, and Ebstein-like tricuspid malformation are common. In d-TGA the AV connections are concordant.
exam2.hint: Identify each ventricle morphologically and note which atrium feeds it.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old at 30 weeks has a fetus with a thickened, doming pulmonary valve, a peak velocity of 2.6 m/s with aliasing, a dilated main pulmonary artery, and forward flow in the ductus arteriosus. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Valvar pulmonary stenosis with post-stenotic dilation

exam2.explanation: A doming, thickened valve with a high-velocity jet and post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery is typical of valvar pulmonary stenosis; forward valve and ductal flow exclude atresia. Absent pulmonary valve shows free regurgitation with aneurysmal branches.
exam2.hint: Use the direction of ductal and valve flow to decide whether the valve is atretic, absent, or narrowed.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old at 24 weeks has a five-chamber view showing a defect in the upper ventricular septum immediately beneath the aortic valve and adjacent to the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. The aorta is not overriding. Which VSD type is most likely?
exam2.explanation: Perimembranous VSDs lie in the membranous septum just below the aortic valve and next to the tricuspid septal leaflet, best seen in the five-chamber view. Doubly committed defects sit beneath both semilunar valves with absent conal septum.
exam2.hint: Locate the defect relative to the aortic valve and the tricuspid septal leaflet.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old at 22 weeks has a fetus with normal chromosomal microarray and an isolated 1.5-mm apical muscular VSD showing low-velocity bidirectional color flow. What is the most appropriate counseling?

options.text: High risk of heart failure in utero
High likelihood of spontaneous closure before or after birth
Need for surgical closure in the newborn period

exam2.explanation: Small isolated muscular VSDs commonly close spontaneously in utero or in the first year and rarely need intervention. Inlet defects and AVSDs, not small muscular VSDs, carry the strong trisomy 21 association.
exam2.hint: Consider the natural history of small defects surrounded entirely by muscle.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old at 20 weeks has a fetus whose great arteries run parallel. The vessel from the left ventricle courses posteriorly and divides into two branches soon after its origin, and the vessel from the right ventricle gives rise to the head and neck arteries. What is the diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A vessel that bifurcates early is the pulmonary artery, and one with head and neck branches is the aorta; their origin from the left and right ventricles respectively, with parallel courses, defines d-TGA (ventriculoarterial discordance). In truncus a single vessel leaves the heart.
exam2.hint: Identify each artery by its branching pattern, then match it to its ventricle.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old at 20 weeks has a fetus with the aorta and IVC on the same side of the spine with the IVC anterior, the stomach on the right, a complete AVSD, pulmonary atresia, and pulmonary veins draining to an extracardiac confluence. Which diagnosis and postnatal concern are most likely?

options.text: Left atrial isomerism with polysplenia and heart block
Situs inversus totalis with low risk of CHD
Right atrial isomerism with asplenia and risk of serious infection

exam2.explanation: Juxtaposition of the aorta and IVC, AVSD, pulmonary outflow obstruction, and TAPVR are typical of right isomerism, which is usually associated with asplenia, requiring antibiotic prophylaxis. Left isomerism features an interrupted IVC with azygos continuation and heart block.
exam2.hint: Note the relationship of the abdominal great vessels and the pulmonary venous drainage.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old with phenylketonuria who has not followed her diet has a markedly elevated phenylalanine level at conception. Which fetal risks are most expected?

options.text: Congenital heart defects such as tetralogy or coarctation, plus microcephaly

exam2.explanation: Maternal PKU with high phenylalanine is teratogenic, causing CHD (often tetralogy, VSD, coarctation), microcephaly, and growth restriction; strict dietary control before conception reduces the risk. Rhabdomyomas relate to tuberous sclerosis.
exam2.hint: Uncontrolled maternal metabolic disease acts as a first-trimester teratogen.

exam2.question: Monochorionic diamniotic twins at 20 weeks: the recipient has polyhydramnios (deepest pocket 9 cm) and a reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus, the donor has oligohydramnios (deepest pocket 1.5 cm) with a visible bladder, and neither twin is hydropic. What is the Quintero stage?
exam2.explanation: Quintero stage III is assigned when either twin has critically abnormal Doppler, such as absent or reversed UA diastolic flow, a reversed DV a-wave, or pulsatile umbilical venous flow, regardless of bladder visibility. Stage II requires a non-visualized donor bladder; stage IV adds hydrops.
exam2.hint: Work through the Quintero criteria in order: fluid discordance, donor bladder, Doppler findings, hydrops, demise.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old at 26 weeks has a fetus with massive cardiomegaly, a markedly enlarged right atrium, and severe tricuspid regurgitation; the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve attaches far more apically than the mitral valve hinge point. What is the diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Ebstein anomaly is apical displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets, creating an atrialized right ventricle with severe regurgitation and right atrial enlargement. In tricuspid valve dysplasia the leaflets are abnormal but attach at the normal annulus.
exam2.hint: Compare the hinge points of the two AV valves on the septum.

exam2.question: A sonographer wants to demonstrate pulmonary venous return into the fetal left atrium with color Doppler. Which setting is most appropriate?

options.text: A high velocity scale of about 80-100 cm/s
A high wall filter to reduce flash artifact
A color box covering the entire thorax
A low velocity scale of about 20-30 cm/s

exam2.explanation: Pulmonary venous flow is low velocity, so a low scale (Nyquist) and low wall filter are needed to display it; high scales and filters will miss these signals. A small color box preserves frame rate.
exam2.hint: Match the color scale to the expected flow velocity.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old at 25 weeks has a fetus with ascites and skin edema only. Which definition of fetal hydrops does this satisfy?

options.text: Any single fluid collection larger than 5 mm
Fluid in three compartments with polyhydramnios
Abnormal fluid in two or more fetal compartments
Skin edema alone thicker than 3 mm

exam2.explanation: Hydrops is defined as abnormal fluid in at least two compartments: ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, or skin edema. Polyhydramnios and placental thickening are often present but are not required.
exam2.hint: Count the compartments involved.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old at 34 weeks has a fetus with tetralogy of Fallot. The pulmonary valve is mildly small, there is antegrade flow across the right ventricular outflow tract, and ductal flow runs from the pulmonary artery to the aorta. What is the most likely postnatal implication?

options.text: Ductal-dependent pulmonary circulation requiring prostaglandin at birth
Pulmonary flow not dependent on the ductus, with elective repair likely
Need for immediate balloon atrial septostomy
Airway compression from aneurysmal pulmonary arteries

exam2.explanation: Antegrade flow across the right outflow with normal pulmonary-to-aortic ductal flow indicates adequate antegrade pulmonary supply, so the newborn is unlikely to depend on the ductus and typically undergoes elective repair; reversed (aorta-to-pulmonary) ductal flow would instead predict prostaglandin dependence. Septostomy is for transposition mixing, and airway compression is a feature of absent pulmonary valve.
exam2.hint: Use the direction of ductal flow to judge whether antegrade pulmonary supply is adequate.

exam2.question: A 33-year-old at 21 weeks has a four-chamber view in which the lower atrial septum adjacent to the crux is absent, both AV valves insert at the same level, two separate AV valve orifices are seen, and the ventricular septum is intact. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Partial atrioventricular septal defect with an ostium primum ASD

exam2.explanation: A partial (incomplete) AVSD has a primum ASD at the crux, two AV valve orifices, loss of normal offset, and no ventricular-level shunt; the left AV valve often has a cleft. A complete AVSD has a common valve with an inlet VSD.
exam2.hint: Count the AV valve orifices and check whether the defect extends to the ventricular level.

exam2.question: During a fetal echo, the fetal spine is directly anterior at the 12 o'clock position and shadows the heart. What is the best approach?

options.text: Increase acoustic output to penetrate the spine
Wait for fetal movement or reposition the mother to change fetal position

exam2.explanation: Ribs and spine anterior to the heart cause acoustic shadowing that output and gain cannot overcome; changing maternal position, waiting, or scanning from a different window lets the fetus turn. Increasing output also conflicts with ALARA.
exam2.hint: Consider why bone shadowing cannot be overcome by processing or output changes.

exam2.question: A 33-year-old at 26 weeks has a fetus with a VSD and overriding aorta, markedly dilated main and branch pulmonary arteries, and to-and-fro flow across a rudimentary pulmonary valve ring. The ductus arteriosus cannot be found. What is the diagnosis and the main postnatal concern?

options.text: Truncus arteriosus with truncal regurgitation and early heart failure
Tetralogy with absent pulmonary valve, with risk of airway compression
Pulmonary atresia with collaterals and severe cyanosis
Idiopathic pulmonary artery dilation with no clinical effect

exam2.explanation: Absent pulmonary valve syndrome produces free pulmonary regurgitation and aneurysmal pulmonary arteries that compress the bronchi, causing respiratory compromise; the ductus is usually absent and 22q11.2 deletion is common. In truncus there is a single outflow valve rather than separate aortic and pulmonary roots.
exam2.hint: Focus on the to-and-fro flow at a rudimentary valve ring and the missing ductus.

exam2.question: While imaging a fetal heart beating at 150 bpm, the frame rate is only 18 Hz with a wide sector and three focal zones. What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Add more focal zones to improve resolution
Increase persistence to smooth the image
Widen the sector to include the whole abdomen
Narrow the sector, reduce depth, and use a single focal zone

exam2.explanation: Frame rate rises when fewer scan lines and less depth are needed per frame, so a narrow sector, minimal depth, and one focal zone improve temporal resolution for the rapidly moving fetal heart. Persistence averages frames and blurs fast motion.
exam2.hint: Frame rate depends on how many lines and how much depth each frame requires.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old at 28 weeks has fetal left ventricular Doppler intervals of 40 ms isovolumetric contraction time, 45 ms isovolumetric relaxation time, and 170 ms ejection time. What is the myocardial performance index?
exam2.explanation: The MPI (Tei index) equals the sum of isovolumetric contraction and relaxation times divided by ejection time: (40 + 45) / 170 = 0.50. Higher values indicate worse combined systolic and diastolic function; 0.24 uses only the contraction time.
exam2.hint: Add both isovolumetric intervals before dividing.

exam2.question: A ductus venosus waveform in a 30-week fetus appears to show absent flow during atrial contraction, but the signal near the baseline looks cut off and the wall filter is set high. What is the best next step?

options.text: Lower the wall filter and repeat the measurement
Report an absent a-wave and refer urgently
Enlarge the gate to include the IVC

exam2.explanation: A high wall filter removes low-velocity signals and can falsely create an apparently absent a-wave; venous Doppler requires a low filter. Enlarging the gate to include the IVC contaminates the signal with a different waveform.
exam2.hint: Filters intended to remove wall motion can also remove genuine slow flow.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old at 37 weeks carries a fetus with d-TGA and intact ventricular septum. The foramen ovale is small with a thickened, immobile septum primum, and the ductus arteriosus is narrow. What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Routine delivery at a community hospital with outpatient follow-up
Prompt induction at the local hospital with neonatal transfer only if cyanosis develops
Maternal digoxin therapy to improve mixing
Delivery at a center able to perform immediate balloon atrial septostomy

exam2.explanation: In d-TGA the circulations run in parallel and survival after birth depends on atrial-level mixing; a restrictive foramen ovale predicts severe hypoxemia requiring emergent balloon atrial septostomy. Digoxin has no effect on mixing.
exam2.hint: After birth these parallel circulations need a place to mix blood.

exam2.question: Why is dextro-transposition of the great arteries frequently missed when screening relies on the four-chamber view alone?

options.text: The ventricles appear reversed in position
The lesion develops only after 30 weeks
The four-chamber view is usually normal
The cardiac axis is usually shifted to the right

exam2.explanation: Because the atrioventricular connections are normal in d-TGA, the four-chamber view looks normal; outflow tract and three-vessel views reveal parallel great arteries or only two vessels in the upper mediastinum. The lesion is present from early development.
exam2.hint: The abnormality lies in the arterial connections, not the inflow.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old at 22 weeks is found to have no identifiable ductus venosus; the umbilical vein bypasses the liver and drains directly into the right atrium, and the heart is enlarged. Which is the most likely diagnosis and concern?

options.text: Persistent right umbilical vein, a benign variant
Agenesis of the ductus venosus with cardiac volume overload

exam2.explanation: Agenesis of the ductus venosus with extrahepatic drainage delivers umbilical return to the heart without the normal resistance, causing volume overload, cardiomegaly, and possible hydrops; it is also associated with aneuploidy and other anomalies. A persistent right umbilical vein still drains through the liver.
exam2.hint: Without its normal regulating shunt, placental return reaches the heart unchecked.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old whose brother died suddenly at age 22 has a 32-week fetus with a sustained heart rate of 105-110 bpm, 1:1 AV conduction, and a normal heart, plus brief runs in which the ventricular rate exceeds the atrial rate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Persistent mild sinus bradycardia below the expected range, episodes of ventricular tachycardia, and a family history of sudden death suggest congenital long QT syndrome; fetal magnetocardiography or postnatal ECG confirms it. Blocked bigeminy would show premature nonconducted atrial beats.
exam2.hint: Combine the sustained mild bradycardia, the runs of a faster ventricular rhythm, and the family history of sudden death.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old at 24 weeks has a fetus with a small, hypertrophied right ventricle, no forward flow across the pulmonary valve, reversed ductal flow, a small tricuspid valve, and color flow within the right ventricular myocardium communicating with the coronary arteries. Which finding is most important for surgical planning?

options.text: Ventriculocoronary connections suggesting right-ventricle-dependent coronary circulation

exam2.explanation: In pulmonary atresia with intact septum, high right ventricular pressure can maintain sinusoids to the coronary arteries; if coronary flow depends on the right ventricle, decompression is dangerous and single-ventricle palliation or transplant may be needed. Tricuspid size and sinusoids guide whether biventricular repair is possible.
exam2.hint: Ask what happens to coronary perfusion if a high-pressure chamber is decompressed.

exam2.question: A 35-year-old at 24 weeks has a fetus with a VSD and overriding aorta, no identifiable main pulmonary artery or ductus arteriosus, and several tortuous vessels arising from the descending aorta and coursing toward the lungs. What is the source of pulmonary blood flow?

options.text: Branch pulmonary arteries arising from a truncus

exam2.explanation: In pulmonary atresia with VSD and no ductus, the lungs are supplied by MAPCAs from the descending aorta. In truncus arteriosus the branch pulmonary arteries arise from the ascending common trunk, not from the descending aorta.
exam2.hint: Trace where the vessels to the lungs originate.

exam2.question: Which postnatal surgical pathway is standard for hypoplastic left heart syndrome?

options.text: Arterial switch operation in the newborn period
Ross procedure followed by coarctation repair
Rastelli procedure with right ventricle-to-pulmonary conduit
Norwood or hybrid procedure, then bidirectional Glenn, then Fontan
